lessons.title: Russia in 1894: Economy and Society
lessons.description: Industrial growth, peasant villages and city slums under the last Tsar's vast empire.
lessons.content_html:
An Empire Built on Contradictions

When Nicholas II became Tsar in 1894, he inherited the largest land empire on Earth — over 22 million square kilometres stretching from Poland to the Pacific. Roughly 125 million people lived under his rule, but only one in seven were ethnic Russians. The rest were Poles, Finns, Ukrainians, Jews, Muslims of Central Asia and dozens of other groups, often resentful of Russification imposed from St Petersburg. Russia was not one society — it was several, held together by the army and the Orthodox Church.

Key Fact

By 1894 the Russian Empire covered roughly one-sixth of the world's land surface and held about 125 million people. Around 80% were peasants, most of them illiterate and tied to their village. Less than 4% lived in cities of over 100,000.

Witte and the Industrial Surge

Russia in 1894 was racing to catch up with the industrial powers of Western Europe. The man driving that race was Sergei Witte, Finance Minister from 1892 to 1903. Witte borrowed heavily from French banks, introduced the gold standard in 1897, and protected Russian industry behind high tariffs. His flagship project was the Trans-Siberian Railway, started in 1891 and largely complete by 1904.

The results were striking. Coal output in the Donbas tripled in the 1890s; oil production in Baku briefly overtook the United States; new steel mills rose in Yekaterinoslav. By 1914 Russia was the world’s fourth largest industrial economy. But the surge was lopsided. Foreign investors owned almost half of Russian heavy industry, and growth concentrated in a handful of cities — St Petersburg, Moscow, Warsaw, Riga — leaving most of the empire untouched.

Between 1890 and 1900 Russian industrial output grew at roughly 8% a year — faster than any other major economy. Railway track doubled from about 30,000 km in 1890 to over 60,000 km by 1905. Witte funded this expansion partly through high indirect taxes on vodka, sugar and matches, which fell hardest on the peasantry. Critics inside the court called him ‘the German’ for borrowing capitalist methods; supporters argued he was the only person preventing Russia from slipping behind Britain, France and Germany permanently.

Life in the New Cities

The factories of St Petersburg and Moscow drew hundreds of thousands of peasants off the land. By 1900 the Russian working class — the proletariat — numbered around three million. Their lives were brutal. A typical Putilov metalworker in St Petersburg worked an 11-hour day, six days a week, for wages well below those of a German or British equivalent. Workers slept in dormitories called artel houses, often eight or ten to a room, with shared bunks taken in shifts.

Trade unions and strikes were illegal. The Okhrana watched factory floors for agitators. When workers did organise, employers responded with mass dismissals and the army with rifles — as students would soon see at Bloody Sunday in 1905. The conditions made urban Russia the natural recruiting ground for the revolutionary parties that would dominate the next twenty years.

The Peasant Majority

Eighty per cent of Russians lived in villages, mostly in European Russia between the Volga and the western frontier. Although serfdom had been abolished in 1861, freedom came at a price. Peasants had to pay redemption payments for the land they had been freed onto, often for forty-nine years. Most land was held collectively by the village commune, the mir, which decided each year which strips each family farmed.

The mir was deeply conservative. Strips were narrow and scattered to share good soil fairly, which made modern farming almost impossible. Population growth meant strips shrank with every generation. Famine in 1891–92 killed between 400,000 and half a million peasants. Many viewed the Tsar as the ‘Little Father’ who would one day give them more land — a hope that the state cynically encouraged.

At the top sat about 1% of the population: the nobility, who owned around a quarter of the land and dominated the army officer corps and the higher civil service. Below them, a small middle class — perhaps 1.5% — of factory owners, merchants, lawyers and doctors, often resentful that political power was closed to them. The urban proletariat was around 4% but growing fast. Beneath everyone else, the peasants — over 80% — whose labour fed the cities and whose grain exports paid for Witte's loans.

Key Fact

Russian agriculture was uniquely backward in 1894 because of redemption payments, the mir’s strip-farming system, and rapid population growth that shrank each family’s share. Famines in 1891 and 1901 showed how thin the margin of survival was.

A Society Primed for Revolution

Witte’s industrial drive built a modern economy on top of a medieval social order. The same railway that carried Donbas coal to St Petersburg also brought Marxist pamphlets to factory dormitories. The same peasants whose grain paid for the loans starved when the harvest failed. By the time Nicholas II had been on the throne for ten years, Russia was producing both steel and revolutionaries faster than it could absorb either. Historians often describe pre-1905 Russia as a country with an early-twentieth-century economy and a seventeenth-century political system — a contradiction the next chapter would test to destruction.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For interpretation questions on late-Tsarist Russia, examiners reward students who can characterise the writer’s school of thought rather than just describing what the source says. A liberal Western historian like Pipes will stress the gap between elite progress and peasant misery; a Soviet-era writer will emphasise the inevitability of revolutionary class struggle. Always test the interpretation against precise contextual knowledge — statistics from Witte’s programme, redemption payments, the 1891 famine — rather than repeating phrases from the source.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Russia in 1894 was the largest land empire on Earth but extremely uneven — a small modern industrial sector in a few cities, surrounded by an enormous, impoverished peasant majority.
  • Witte’s industrialisation made Russia the world’s fourth largest industrial economy by 1914, but it relied on foreign loans, peasant taxes and brutal urban working conditions.
  • Redemption payments, the mir and famines kept the peasantry poor and resentful, while the new urban proletariat became fertile ground for revolutionary politics.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A is from the British historian Orlando Figes (A People’s Tragedy, 1996), arguing that Witte’s industrialisation papered over deep peasant misery. Interpretation B is from the Soviet-era textbook A Short History of the USSR (1965), arguing that Witte’s reforms created the modern proletariat that would carry through the revolution.
Identify two ways in which the interpretations of Russia’s economy in 1894 differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Figes presents industrialisation as a top-down imposition that left the peasantry impoverished, while the Soviet text presents it as the necessary precondition for working-class revolution.
• Figes emphasises the human cost (famines, factory conditions, debt), while the Soviet text emphasises the achievement of building a modern proletariat.
• Figes is critical of the regime that drove the change; the Soviet text frames the same change as historically progressive.

Mastering: Two precise differences identified with exact reference to both interpretations.
Secure: Two clear differences identified, each rooted in the interpretations.
Developing: One clear difference plus a vague second point.
Emerging: General comments about the interpretations without identifying specific differences.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A is from the British historian Orlando Figes (1996). Interpretation B is from the Soviet-era textbook A Short History of the USSR (1965).
Suggest one reason why these two interpretations of Witte’s industrialisation differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• The interpretations differ in purpose: Figes is writing a critical history for a Western readership, while the Soviet textbook is teaching a generation of Soviet schoolchildren to see industrialisation as the prelude to socialism.
• They differ in time of writing: Figes wrote after the collapse of the USSR with full archival access, while the Soviet text was produced under censorship that demanded a Marxist framework.
• They use different evidence: Figes draws on peasant memoirs and famine statistics; the Soviet text foregrounds factory output figures and union membership.
• They reflect different traditions of historiography — the liberal/Western and the Soviet/orthodox schools.

Mastering: A clearly explained reason linked to purpose, evidence, time of writing or perspective, with specific support.
Secure: A clear reason explained with reference to both interpretations.
Developing: A reason identified but not fully developed.
Emerging: General comment about disagreement without explanation.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A claims that ‘Russia in 1894 was a backward society where industrial growth only deepened the misery of the peasantry.’
How convincing is this interpretation about Russia in 1894? Use Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge to evaluate.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Arguments that the interpretation is convincing:
• Redemption payments kept peasants in debt for decades after the 1861 Emancipation; the 1891 famine killed up to 500,000.
• Witte’s reliance on indirect taxes on vodka, sugar and matches fell hardest on the peasants.
• The mir’s strip-farming system blocked productivity gains and shrank with every generation.

Arguments against:
• By 1914 Russia was the world’s fourth largest industrial economy — the change was real and rapid.
• New urban opportunities, however brutal, drew millions off subsistence farms by choice.
• Some peasant regions, especially the Black Earth zone, exported grain successfully.

Mastering: A substantiated evaluation that uses precise contextual knowledge to test the interpretation and reaches a clear judgement.
Secure: A clear evaluation supported by relevant detail on both sides.
Developing: An attempt to evaluate with limited contextual support.
Emerging: Description of the interpretation without independent evaluation.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Sergei Witte’s industrial policies on Russia between 1892 and 1903.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Industrial output grew at roughly 8% a year in the 1890s, making Russia the fourth largest industrial economy by 1914.
• The Trans-Siberian Railway opened Siberia to settlement and trade, and tied the empire together militarily.
• The gold standard (1897) and high tariffs attracted French and Belgian investment but increased foreign ownership of heavy industry.
• Indirect taxes on peasants funded the loans, deepening rural poverty and discontent.
• The growth of the urban proletariat created the social base for the revolutionary parties that emerged after 1898.

Mastering: A chain of consequences explained, linking economic, social and political effects.
Secure: Two or more developed effects supported by specific evidence.
Developing: One developed effect plus simple identification of others.
Emerging: General descriptive comments about Russian industry.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘Russia in 1894 was held back more by its rural society than by its political system.’
How far do you accept this view of Russia in 1894? In your answer you should:
• consider the rural society of 1894
• consider the political system of 1894
• reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Arguments for rural society holding Russia back:
• Redemption payments and the mir blocked agricultural reform.
• 80% of the population were peasants, most illiterate and resistant to change.
• Famines (1891) showed the fragility of the rural economy.

Arguments for the political system holding Russia back:
• Autocracy excluded talent — the small middle class had no political voice.
• No legal trade unions, no parliament, no free press limited the safety valves available to other industrialising states.
• Witte’s programme could not be sustained politically because the Tsar resented modernising ministers.

Judgement should weigh both factors against each other rather than describing them in turn.

Mastering: A substantiated judgement weighing both factors with precise evidence.
Secure: A clear argument addressing both factors with relevant evidence.
Developing: Description of both factors with limited weighing.
Emerging: Narrative on one factor only.
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of life in the cities of St Petersburg and Moscow on Russian factory workers by 1900.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Long hours (typically 11 hours, six days a week) and low wages produced widespread exhaustion and poor health.
• Overcrowded artel dormitories spread disease and broke up family life as men migrated alone from the village.
• Bans on trade unions and strikes pushed worker grievances underground and into illegal political organisations.
• The Okhrana’s surveillance and the army’s readiness to fire on protesters made revolutionary parties the only safe outlet for protest.
• Concentration in factories like the Putilov works in St Petersburg made coordinated mass action possible — this would matter in 1905 and 1917.

Mastering: A chain of consequences linking working conditions to political radicalisation.
Secure: Two or more developed effects with specific support.
Developing: One developed effect; others mentioned only briefly.
Emerging: General description of factory life without explanation of effects.
[8 marks]

lessons.title: Nicholas II's Autocracy and Opposition
lessons.description: How autocracy, the Okhrana and the Orthodox Church faced liberal and revolutionary challenge.
lessons.content_html:
A Sacred Duty

Nicholas II did not become a tyrant by choice. He became one by inheritance and conviction. His father Alexander III had reversed liberal reforms after the assassination of Alexander II in 1881 and trained Nicholas to see autocracy as a religious duty owed to God and ancestor. The official slogan of the regime — ‘Orthodoxy, Autocracy, Nationality’ — treated the Tsar as the divinely appointed Father of his people. Nicholas wrote in his diary that constitutional government would be ‘senseless dreams’. The problem was that the empire he inherited was no longer a society in which such an idea could survive.

Key Fact

The Tsarist regime rested on three pillars summarised in the slogan ‘Orthodoxy, Autocracy, Nationality’. The Orthodox Church taught obedience to the Tsar; the Tsar ruled without parliament or written constitution; and Russification subordinated minority peoples to Russian identity.

The Court and the Tsarina

Nicholas’s court was small, traditional and increasingly cut off from real political life. Senior posts went to relatives and trusted nobles rather than expert administrators. His wife Tsarina Alexandra, a German-born princess who converted to Orthodoxy, was devoutly religious and politically inflexible. Together they preferred quiet family life at Tsarskoe Selo to the public ceremonies of capital politics. As the years went on, real decision-making shrank to a tiny circle of intimates — a vulnerability that the war years would expose disastrously.

The Okhrana and the Police State

Behind the spiritual rhetoric stood a police state. The Okhrana was the secret police arm of the Ministry of the Interior. Created after the assassination of Alexander II in 1881, it ran agents inside the universities, the factories and even the revolutionary parties themselves. By 1900 the Okhrana had infiltrated the Bolsheviks so deeply that one of Lenin’s closest collaborators, Roman Malinovsky, was a paid agent passing names to the police.

Punishment was harsh but selective. The regime preferred to send agitators to Siberian exile rather than create martyrs. Lenin himself spent three years in Shushenskoe between 1897 and 1900, free to read and write but cut off from political action. The Okhrana also relied on censorship of newspapers, the banning of trade unions and laws against public meetings of more than three people without permission.

The Russian Orthodox Church was effectively a department of state, run by the Tsar’s Holy Synod and headed by a layman, the Procurator. Priests were paid by the government and were expected to denounce political agitators in their parishes. Russification — banning the Polish language in schools, restricting Jewish residence to the Pale of Settlement, suppressing Finnish autonomy — was meant to bind the empire together. In practice it created angry educated minorities, especially Poles and Jews, who would supply many of the empire’s most determined revolutionaries. Pogroms against Jewish communities, often tolerated by local police, drove waves of emigration to Britain and America.

Liberal Opposition

Not all opposition was revolutionary. Russia’s small middle class — doctors, lawyers, university professors, factory owners — mostly wanted what western liberals wanted: a parliament, a constitution, civil rights. They expressed themselves through the zemstva (rural councils) and through professional associations. Their political home from 1905 onwards would be the Constitutional Democrats or Kadets, led by the historian Pavel Milyukov, who wanted a British-style parliamentary monarchy.

A more conservative liberal current, the Octobrists, was content to accept the limited reforms Nicholas would offer in 1905 and stop there. Both groups posed a problem for Nicholas: they were patriotic and respectable, so persecution looked unjust, but their demands meant the end of pure autocracy.

Revolutionary Opposition

More dangerous, in the regime’s eyes, were the revolutionary parties. The Socialist Revolutionaries, formed in 1901, drew on the older Russian populist tradition of going ‘to the people’. They believed the peasantry, not the proletariat, would lead the revolution and used political assassination as a tactic — murdering ministers and grand dukes through their ‘Combat Organisation’. Two interior ministers, Sipyagin in 1902 and Plehve in 1904, were among their victims.

The Russian Social Democratic Labour Party, founded in 1898, was Marxist and looked to the urban working class. At its Second Congress in London and Brussels in 1903 it split. Lenin demanded a small, disciplined party of full-time professional revolutionaries; Julius Martov wanted a mass party along German socialist lines. Lenin’s faction won a procedural vote — hence the name Bolsheviks, ‘majoritarians’ — while Martov’s group became the Mensheviks. The split would shape the revolutions to come.

The label ‘Bolshevik’ (majority) referred only to a single vote at the 1903 Congress, on which faction would control the editorial board of the party newspaper. Until 1917 the Mensheviks were generally larger than the Bolsheviks inside Russia. But the Bolshevik label stuck, giving Lenin’s faction a useful claim to legitimacy. Until 1912 the two groups were technically still one party; the formal break came at the Prague Conference. This is why students should not assume a sharp Bolshevik–Menshevik divide before 1914 — many local activists moved between the factions.

Key Fact

By 1903 there were four main opposition currents: the Kadets (liberal, parliamentary), the Octobrists (conservative liberal), the Socialist Revolutionaries (peasant-focused, used assassination), and the Social Democrats — split into Bolsheviks under Lenin and Mensheviks under Martov.

Why It Mattered

In 1894 the regime believed it could ride out criticism through the Okhrana, the Church and the army. By 1904 Russia had assassins inside the cabinet, Marxist printing presses inside its factories and a Tsar still convinced that constitutional government was a ‘senseless dream’. The system that looked unshakeable to Nicholas in his Tsarskoe Selo study was already cracking on the streets of St Petersburg. The next blow — Bloody Sunday — would come from outside the political parties altogether, but the parties would be ready to exploit it.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Examiners reward students who can distinguish between the different opposition groups rather than treating them as a single ‘the revolutionaries’. For interpretation questions, recognise that a totalitarian-school historian (like Conquest) will read 1903 as the moment Lenin built the dictatorial party that would later become Stalin’s; a revisionist will stress how small and divided the Bolsheviks really were before 1917. Use precise contextual knowledge — the 1903 vote in London, Malinovsky as an Okhrana agent — to test the interpretation.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Nicholas II saw autocracy as a religious duty inherited from his father; the regime’s ideology was ‘Orthodoxy, Autocracy, Nationality’ and rested on the Church and the Okhrana.
  • Liberal opposition (Kadets, Octobrists) wanted a parliamentary monarchy; revolutionary opposition was split between the peasant-focused Socialist Revolutionaries and the Marxist Social Democrats.
  • The 1903 split between Bolsheviks and Mensheviks divided the Marxist movement over how to organise — a small disciplined cadre versus a mass party — and would shape the revolutions of 1917.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A is from the British historian Robert Service (Lenin: A Biography, 2000), arguing that Lenin’s 1903 demand for a small disciplined party showed his authoritarian instincts from the start. Interpretation B is from the American revisionist historian Lars Lih (Lenin Rediscovered, 2006), arguing that Lenin’s 1903 position was a normal Marxist response to operating under Tsarist police repression.
Identify two ways in which the interpretations differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Service presents Lenin as authoritarian by temperament; Lih presents him as a pragmatic Marxist responding to Russian conditions.
• Service emphasises continuity with the later one-party state; Lih emphasises the influence of German Social Democracy on Lenin’s thought.
• Service blames Lenin personally; Lih blames the Tsarist police state for forcing underground organisation.

Mastering: Two precise differences identified with reference to both interpretations.
Secure: Two clear differences identified, each rooted in the interpretations.
Developing: One clear difference plus a vague second point.
Emerging: General comments without specific differences.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why these two interpretations of the 1903 split differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Different evidence: Service emphasises Lenin’s polemics; Lih draws on Lenin’s own footnotes citing German socialists.
• Different traditions of historiography: Service draws on a liberal-Western reading; Lih is part of a revisionist re-reading of Lenin.
• Different time of writing: Lih’s book responds to thirty years of revisionist scholarship since the opening of Soviet archives.
• Different purposes: Service is writing for a general readership and giving a clear moral judgement; Lih is writing a specialist re-evaluation.

Mastering: A clear reason explained with reference to purpose, evidence or time of writing, with specific support.
Secure: A clear reason explained with reference to both interpretations.
Developing: A reason identified but not fully developed.
Emerging: General comment without explanation.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A claims that ‘Tsarist Russia in the early 1900s was effectively a police state, with all opposition either driven underground or assassinated.’
How convincing is this interpretation about Tsarist Russia before 1905? Use Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge to evaluate.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Arguments that the interpretation is convincing:
• The Okhrana ran extensive networks of informants and infiltrated the Bolsheviks (e.g. Malinovsky).
• Trade unions and political parties were illegal; meetings of more than three required police permission.
• Socialist Revolutionary assassinations — Sipyagin (1902), Plehve (1904), Grand Duke Sergei (1905) — show how violent the politics had become.

Arguments that it is less convincing:
• Liberal zemstva, professional associations and a critical press operated at the limits of legality.
• Exile, not execution, was the standard punishment for political crime; Lenin spent three years writing in Shushenskoe.
• A small but real middle class debated reform openly, especially after the 1891 famine relief campaign.

Mastering: A substantiated evaluation testing the interpretation against precise contextual knowledge.
Secure: A clear evaluation supported by relevant detail on both sides.
Developing: An attempt to evaluate with limited contextual support.
Emerging: Description of the interpretation without independent evaluation.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the 1903 split in the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party between Bolsheviks and Mensheviks.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• The split divided the Marxist opposition for fifteen years, weakening it during the 1905 Revolution and again in early 1917.
• It produced two competing models of revolutionary organisation — Lenin’s small disciplined cadre and Martov’s mass party.
• It explains why the Bolsheviks were able to act decisively in October 1917 when other socialist groups hesitated.
• It set the precedent for one-party rule, since Lenin had spent fourteen years arguing that purity mattered more than unity.
• It pushed the Mensheviks into permanent opposition after 1917 — many were arrested or exiled in the 1920s.

Mastering: A chain of consequences explained, linking 1903 to 1917 and beyond.
Secure: Two or more developed effects supported by specific evidence.
Developing: One developed effect plus simple identification of others.
Emerging: General comments about disunity.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘The greatest threat to Tsarist autocracy before 1905 came from liberal opposition rather than revolutionary parties.’
How far do you accept this view? In your answer you should:
• consider the strength of liberal opposition before 1905
• consider the strength of revolutionary opposition before 1905
• reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Arguments for liberal opposition being the greater threat:

• Liberal demands for a Duma and constitution would, if conceded, end pure autocracy.

Arguments for revolutionary parties being the greater threat:
• Socialist Revolutionary assassinations directly killed senior officials.
• The Marxist parties built networks inside the new factory cities.
• The 1903 split made the Bolsheviks more disciplined, not weaker.

Judgement should weigh the immediate physical threat against the long-term political threat.

Mastering: Substantiated judgement weighing both factors with precise evidence.
Secure: Clear argument addressing both factors with relevant evidence.
Developing: Description of both with limited weighing.
Emerging: Narrative on one factor only.
[12 marks]

lessons.title: The 1905 Revolution and October Manifesto
lessons.description: Bloody Sunday, soviets and a Tsar forced to grant a parliament he did not want.
lessons.content_html:
Defeat in the East

In 1904 Nicholas II went to war with Japan over influence in Manchuria and Korea. Senior ministers expected a quick victory that would, in Interior Minister Plehve’s phrase, give Russia ‘a small victorious war’ to distract a restless population. Instead the Russian Pacific squadron was destroyed at Port Arthur, the Baltic fleet sailed halfway round the world only to be annihilated at Tsushima in May 1905, and the army lost the land battle of Mukden. By spring 1905 Russia had lost a war to an Asian power for the first time in the modern era. The political shockwave at home was immediate: defeat exposed the autocracy as incompetent as well as repressive.

Key Fact

The Russo-Japanese War of 1904–05 ended in three humiliating defeats — Port Arthur, Mukden and Tsushima — and discredited the autocracy at the moment that domestic discontent was spilling onto the streets.

Bloody Sunday

On a freezing Sunday morning in January 1905, around 150,000 striking workers and their families marched through St Petersburg to the Winter Palace. They were led by Father Georgi Gapon, an Orthodox priest who ran a police-approved workers’ assembly. They carried icons and portraits of the Tsar, sang hymns, and bore a respectful petition asking for an eight-hour day, fairer wages and a constituent assembly. Nicholas was not in the city. The Imperial Guard, drawn up around the Palace Square, opened fire on the procession.

Official figures admitted to about 100 dead; eyewitnesses and later historians put the toll at over 200, possibly up to 1,000 including those who died of wounds. The day became known as Bloody Sunday. The political effect was incalculable. Workers who had marched believing in the ‘Little Father’ left convinced he had personally ordered the massacre. Lenin, in exile, called it ‘the awakening of Russia’.

Revolution Spreads

By summer 1905 strikes had paralysed industrial Russia. Peasants burned manor houses across the central provinces. Mutinies broke out in the armed forces, most famously aboard the Black Sea battleship Potemkin in June, where sailors killed officers in protest at maggoty meat. National minorities — Poles, Finns, Georgians — demanded autonomy. Liberal middle-class professionals organised the ‘Union of Unions’ in May, demanding a constituent assembly.

In October a general strike paralysed the railways and printing presses. Workers in St Petersburg formed the city’s first soviet, a council of factory delegates that ran the strike. The young Leon Trotsky, then a Menshevik, became its de facto chair. The state’s authority in the capital had effectively collapsed.

Witte, recalled to government, told Nicholas he had two choices: military dictatorship or a constitution. On 17 October 1905 the Tsar reluctantly issued the October Manifesto, conceding three things: civil rights (freedom of speech, assembly, conscience), legal political parties, and an elected parliament called the Duma. He told his mother he had signed it ‘with sickness in my soul’ and described those who had pushed it on him as traitors. The Manifesto was a strategic retreat, not a conversion to constitutional government.

Why the Autocracy Survived

By October the regime looked finished. Within two months it had won. Three things saved it. First, the October Manifesto split the opposition. Liberals and Octobrists welcomed the concessions; revolutionaries dismissed them. The middle-class moderate base, which had marched alongside workers all summer, now had something to lose by joining a Bolshevik-led uprising.

Second, the Tsar had ended the war. The Treaty of Portsmouth in September brought home the Manchurian field army, who were used to crush the Moscow Uprising in December 1905 with house-to-house artillery. Third, the army itself had stayed loyal. Although there were mutinies in the navy and a few army units, the bulk of the conscript infantry obeyed orders. By March 1906 the St Petersburg Soviet had been arrested, Trotsky among them.

In December 1905, after the moderate liberals had accepted the Manifesto, Bolshevik and Menshevik agitators in Moscow tried to push the revolution further. They built barricades in the working-class Presnya district and called for a general strike. The Tsar sent the elite Semyonovsky Guards Regiment from St Petersburg with field artillery. For nine days, troops shelled the district building by building, killing perhaps 1,000 civilians. The uprising’s defeat broke the back of the 1905 Revolution: it showed that the Manifesto had separated the moderate middle class from any further street fighting, and that the regime would now use overwhelming military force without hesitation. Lenin took two lessons. First, soviets were a powerful institution. Second, an unarmed urban population could not defeat a disciplined army. Both lessons would shape Bolshevik thinking through 1917.

Key Fact

The Tsarist regime survived 1905 because the October Manifesto split moderate opposition from radical revolutionaries, the army stayed loyal, and the war with Japan ended in time to free troops to crush the Moscow Uprising.

Aftermath

Lenin would later call 1905 ‘the dress rehearsal’ for 1917. The phrase captures both the lessons learned and the lessons missed. Workers had discovered the soviet as an institution of mass democracy. Revolutionaries had seen that mutinies in the armed forces were the regime’s nightmare. But the regime had also learned: rapid concession, moral discrediting of the opposition through religious imagery, and a willingness to use overwhelming force once the political moment had passed. The chapter was not closed. The Manifesto’s promise of a Duma still had to be tested, and the next four years — the era of Stolypin — would show how Nicholas planned to honour it.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Examiners frequently set interpretation questions on 1905 because it is the easiest period to misread. Strong answers contrast revolutionary writers (who treat 1905 as a defeated revolution that proved the workers’ potential) with liberal historians (who treat 1905 as a missed opportunity for constitutional reform). For chain-of-consequence questions on Bloody Sunday or the Manifesto, drop the listing habit — explain how military defeat produced strikes, which produced the October Manifesto, which split the opposition, which let the regime use force in December.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Defeat in the Russo-Japanese War (1904–05) discredited the autocracy and turned domestic protest into open revolution after Bloody Sunday in January 1905.
  • The October Manifesto conceded civil rights, legal parties and a Duma. Nicholas signed it under duress and resented it for the rest of his reign.
  • The autocracy survived because the Manifesto split moderate liberals from revolutionaries, the army stayed loyal, and the end of the war freed troops to crush the December uprising in Moscow.

practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the October Manifesto of 1905 on Russian politics.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• It legalised political parties for the first time, allowing the Kadets and Octobrists to organise openly.
• It split the opposition: liberals welcomed the concessions; revolutionaries rejected them, isolating the Bolsheviks.
• It created the Duma, an elected parliament that Nicholas regarded as a temporary nuisance and would shortly try to neutralise (see next lesson).

Emerging: General descriptive comments about the Manifesto.

lessons.title: Stolypin, the Dumas and Reform to 1914
lessons.description: Land reform, the noose, four Dumas and a regime stuck between repression and modernisation.
lessons.content_html:
The Promise Withdrawn

Six months after he had signed the October Manifesto, Nicholas II issued the Fundamental Laws of April 1906. Article 4 stated that ‘Supreme Autocratic Power belongs to the Emperor of All the Russias.’ The Manifesto had hinted at constitutional monarchy. The Fundamental Laws confirmed that Russia was nothing of the sort. The Duma could pass laws, but only if the Tsar approved. He could dissolve it at will, control the military and foreign policy, and rule by decree under Article 87 when it was not sitting. He kept the right to appoint and dismiss ministers. Russia became, in legal terms, a constitutional façade over an autocratic core.

Key Fact

The Fundamental Laws of April 1906 reserved ‘Supreme Autocratic Power’ to the Tsar. He could dissolve the Duma at will, rule by decree under Article 87 between sessions, and appoint and dismiss ministers without consultation. The Duma had legislative initiative but no real power.

Four Dumas in Eleven Years

Between 1906 and 1917 there were four Dumas. Each was less representative than the last because Nicholas changed the electoral rules whenever the result displeased him.

The First Duma (April–July 1906) was elected on a relatively wide franchise. Kadets dominated it and demanded land reform, civil liberties and ministerial accountability. Nicholas dissolved it after seventy-two days. The Second Duma (February–June 1907) was even more radical, with strong showings from Social Revolutionaries and Social Democrats. Nicholas dissolved it under a fabricated charge that Social Democrat deputies were plotting against him — the so-called ‘coup of June 1907’ — and rewrote the franchise to favour the propertied classes.

The Third Duma (1907–1912) was the only one to serve its full five-year term. The new electoral law gave one landlord vote the same weight as 543 peasant votes, producing a body Stolypin could work with. The Fourth Duma (1912–1917) was similarly conservative but increasingly critical of wartime mismanagement; in August 1915 a ‘Progressive Bloc’ of moderate parties demanded a government enjoying public confidence. Nicholas refused. The Fourth Duma would still be sitting, technically, when the Tsar abdicated in March 1917 and its members improvised the Provisional Government.

Three structural problems doomed the Dumas. First, the State Council — an upper house, half appointed by the Tsar — could veto anything the Duma passed. Second, the Tsar held the budget for the army, navy and his own court outside Duma control, removing the parliament’s most powerful weapon in any constitutional system. Third, deputies had no control over ministers, who answered only to the Tsar. The result was a body that could complain but never govern. Liberal historians (Lieven, Pipes) treat the Dumas as a wasted opportunity; revolutionaries treated them as a façade that proved violent revolution was the only route to change.

Stolypin’s Carrot and Stick

In July 1906 Nicholas appointed Pyotr Stolypin as Prime Minister. Stolypin had two beliefs that defined his time in office. First, the regime needed to crush political violence ruthlessly. Second, it needed to create a class of prosperous, conservative peasant smallholders who would be loyal to the throne. He pursued both with equal vigour.

The repressive side became known as Stolypin’s necktie. Field court martials were authorised in 1906 to try suspects accused of political violence. Verdicts had to be delivered within forty-eight hours and executions carried out within twenty-four hours of sentencing. Between 1906 and 1909 around 3,000 people were hanged. Stolypin himself survived an assassination attempt in August 1906 that killed twenty-seven people at his home and wounded his daughter.

The Wager on the Strong

The reforming side was equally radical. Stolypin’s land legislation of 1906–1911 allowed peasants to leave the mir, consolidate their strips into a single farm, and own the land outright. He hoped to create a stratum of prosperous ‘wager-on-the-strong’ peasants who would side with the regime against urban radicalism. About a quarter of European Russian peasant families had left the mir by 1916, more in fertile southern provinces and far fewer in the impoverished north. The remaining redemption payments were abolished in 1907. Industrial growth resumed and grain exports recovered.

Yet the policy had limits. The richest peasants benefited; the poorest often sold their consolidated plots and drifted back into the cities as fresh proletarian recruits. The land hunger that had driven the 1905 jacquerie was not solved — in 1917 peasants would still seize manor estates. Stolypin himself believed he needed twenty years of peace to complete the transformation. He was assassinated by a Socialist Revolutionary at the Kiev Opera in September 1911.

In April 1912, troops fired on a strike of British-owned Lena Goldfield miners in eastern Siberia, killing about 270 unarmed workers. The massacre revived urban militancy and produced a wave of strikes in St Petersburg and Moscow that lasted into 1914. By July 1914 there were strike levels and barricades in the capital comparable to those of 1905, briefly interrupted only by the outbreak of war. The lesson was awkward: Stolypin’s land reform might be working in the countryside, but the cities had returned to the boil.

Key Fact

Stolypin combined harsh repression (around 3,000 hangings via field court martial) with the most ambitious land reform of Tsarism (peasants leaving the mir, redemption payments abolished, ‘wager on the strong’). About a quarter of peasant families had left the mir by 1916, but his death in 1911 cut the experiment short.

A Regime in Stalemate

By 1914 Russia looked superficially stable. Industrial output was rising; the rouble was strong; the Third and Fourth Dumas had not been dissolved. Yet under the surface the political settlement was broken. Stolypin was dead and Nicholas had not replaced him with anyone of comparable energy. The Duma functioned as a debating society, not a government. Strikes were back to 1905 levels. Liberal parties had lost faith in cooperation with the Crown; revolutionaries had lost faith in liberal parties. The regime had survived the storm of 1905 by promising change and then withholding most of it. The next storm — the First World War — would arrive in August 1914 and find an autocracy with no functioning safety valve left.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For interpretations of Stolypin, examiners reward students who can hold his repression and reform together rather than treating him as either a hangman or a moderniser. The classic historiographical contrast is between writers who see his death in 1911 as the moment Tsarism lost its last chance, and those who argue that even with twenty more years his reforms could never have closed the gap with mass urban discontent. For chain-of-consequence questions, link the Fundamental Laws to the dissolution of the First Duma to the changed franchise to the Third Duma’s docility.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Fundamental Laws of April 1906 stripped the October Manifesto of much of its substance, reserving Supreme Autocratic Power to the Tsar and giving him the right to dissolve the Duma at will.
  • Four Dumas sat between 1906 and 1917; the Tsar dissolved the first two and rewrote the franchise to produce more compliant third and fourth chambers.
  • Stolypin combined repression (‘Stolypin’s necktie’, around 3,000 hangings) with the most ambitious land reform of Tsarism. His assassination in 1911 cut the experiment short, and by 1914 urban unrest had returned to 1905 levels.

lessons.title: The First World War and the Fall of the Tsar
lessons.description: Defeats, food queues, Rasputin and the abdication of Nicholas II in March 1917.
lessons.content_html:
A Patriotic Summer

When Russia entered the First World War on 1 August 1914, crowds knelt in Palace Square chanting ‘God save the Tsar’. The strikes that had crippled St Petersburg in July evaporated overnight. The Duma, the Kadets and the Octobrists all voted war credits. Many Bolsheviks were exiled or imprisoned for opposing the war. The capital was renamed from the German-sounding St Petersburg to the Russian Petrograd. For perhaps a month, the regime looked united. Nothing else would go right for Tsarism for the next two-and-a-half years.

Key Fact

Russia entered the First World War in August 1914 in a wave of patriotic enthusiasm; St Petersburg was renamed Petrograd to remove its German sound. The strike wave that had reached 1905 levels by July 1914 collapsed almost completely.

From Tannenberg to Catastrophe

The Russian high command had promised allies they would crush East Prussia within six weeks. They invaded with two armies in mid-August. By the end of the month one had been encircled and destroyed at Tannenberg; its commander, General Samsonov, shot himself. A week later, the second army was driven back at the Masurian Lakes. By 1915 the Russians had been pushed out of Russian Poland, Lithuania and Galicia. The army lost around 1.4 million men killed and wounded in 1915 alone, and another 1.6 million as prisoners. Officer casualties were so high that peasant conscripts were being commanded by sergeants without proper training.

Industry was overwhelmed. Russia produced barely a fifth of the rifles its army needed in 1915. Shells, machine guns, boots and even rifles ran short. Soldiers were sent to the front in pairs with one rifle between two, instructed to pick up the dead man’s weapon. The Brusilov Offensive of 1916 briefly recovered some ground in Galicia at the cost of another million casualties, but it could not be exploited because there were no reserves left.

Russia was the world’s fourth largest industrial economy in 1914 but still concentrated in a handful of cities and dependent on imports. The Baltic was closed by Germany; the Black Sea by Ottoman Turkey from late 1914; only Vladivostok and Murmansk-Archangel remained, and the latter was iced over half the year. Without imported chemicals, machine tools and rolling stock, military production never matched Germany’s. Coal output fell by a third; railways collapsed; food trains rotted in sidings. The collapse of transport, more than the front-line defeats, would eventually starve Petrograd.

The Tsar Takes Command

In September 1915, against the unanimous advice of his ministers, Nicholas dismissed his uncle Grand Duke Nikolai and assumed personal command of the army at Mogilev. The decision was a disaster on two counts. Strategically, Nicholas was no general; in practice his Chief of Staff, Alekseyev, ran the war. Politically, every defeat from now on was personally his. He spent the next eighteen months at headquarters while government in Petrograd was effectively delegated to the Tsarina Alexandra and the small circle around her.

Alexandra and Rasputin

Alexandra was hated for three reasons. She was German by birth, in a country at war with Germany. She was domineering, repeatedly purging capable ministers in favour of nonentities loyal only to her. And she relied on Rasputin, a Siberian peasant holy man who appeared able to ease the haemophilia of the heir Alexei. By 1916, Petrograd was full of stories — many exaggerated, some invented — that Rasputin slept with the Tsarina and chose ministers between drinking bouts.

The damage was less the truth than the perception. Even members of the Romanov family openly accused the Tsarina of treason. In November 1916 the Kadet leader Pavel Milyukov delivered a speech in the Duma listing every disaster of the war and ending each example with the question, ‘Is this stupidity or is it treason?’ In December a group of conservative aristocrats led by Prince Felix Yusupov murdered Rasputin. His body was dumped under the ice of the Neva. The killing only deepened the sense that the dynasty had lost its grip.

Bread, Coal and Bullets

The home front was breaking faster than the front. About 15 million men were conscripted between 1914 and 1917, stripping farms of labour. Inflation rose to 400% by 1917. Real wages collapsed. Bread queues formed before dawn. Coal shortages closed factories and froze homes. Rural conscription disrupted harvests; railway breakdowns left grain rotting in Siberian sidings while Petrograd starved. By February 1917 the official daily bread ration in the capital had fallen below subsistence and was being missed even on that.

On 23 February 1917 (8 March, new style) women textile workers in Vyborg marked International Women’s Day with a bread strike. By 25 February over 200,000 workers were out. On 26 February the Tsar ordered General Khabalov to disperse them by force. Some units obeyed; the Volynsky Regiment refused and joined the protesters on 27 February. Within forty-eight hours the Petrograd garrison — some 160,000 men — had mutinied. The Duma formed a Provisional Committee. Generals at headquarters told Nicholas the army would not fight for him. On 2 March (15 March, new style) Nicholas abdicated, first for himself and then, after his brother refused the throne, for his son too. Three centuries of Romanov rule had ended in five days.

Key Fact

The February Revolution was triggered by women textile workers’ bread strike on International Women’s Day, 23 February 1917 (Old Style). Within five days the Petrograd garrison had mutinied, the Duma had formed a Provisional Committee, and Nicholas had abdicated. The revolution was spontaneous — no political party planned it.

Why It Mattered

The fall of the Tsar was the most surprising political event of the early twentieth century. Lenin, in Zürich, had told an audience two months earlier that he would probably not live to see the revolution. The autocracy collapsed not because revolutionary parties had grown strong but because military defeat, economic strain and the discrediting of the dynasty by Rasputin had hollowed it out from inside. The Tsar abdicated, but the war was still being fought, the cities were still hungry, and the soldiers in the capital had just learned that they could disobey orders. The next chapter would test whether the new Provisional Government could solve any of these problems faster than the Tsar had.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Examiners specifically warn against eyewitness narrative voice on essay questions. Do not write ‘I was a worker in February 1917’ — it kills your AO2 marks. For interpretation questions, contrast a totalitarian-school view (Nicholas’s personal failings caused the collapse) with a structural view (war and economic strain made collapse inevitable, regardless of leadership). For chain-of-consequence questions, link the choice to take command in 1915 to the discrediting of the dynasty by Alexandra and Rasputin to the loss of military and Duma confidence by February 1917.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Russia entered the First World War with patriotic enthusiasm but suffered massive defeats from Tannenberg onwards, losing around three million men killed, wounded or captured by the end of 1915.
  • Nicholas’s decision to take personal command in September 1915 made every defeat his and left government in the hands of Alexandra and Rasputin, destroying public confidence in the dynasty.
  • The February Revolution was a spontaneous mass rising triggered by bread shortages and the Petrograd garrison’s refusal to fire on protesters; Nicholas abdicated on 2 March (15 March, new style), ending three centuries of Romanov rule.

Interpretation B is from the conservative Russian historian Sergei Pushkarev (1963), arguing that the dynasty was destroyed mainly by the personal failings of Nicholas, Alexandra and Rasputin.
Identify two ways in which the interpretations of the fall of the Tsar differ.

Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Read locates the cause in long-term structural strain (war, economy, peasant question); Pushkarev locates it in the personal failings of the imperial family.

• Read emphasises mass forces (workers, soldiers); Pushkarev emphasises individual decisions (taking command, listening to Rasputin).

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A claims that ‘Rasputin’s real influence was modest, but the perception of his hold over the imperial family destroyed public trust in the dynasty.’
How convincing is this interpretation? Use Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge to evaluate.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Arguments that the interpretation is convincing:
• Most ministers were appointed and dismissed by Alexandra rather than Rasputin himself; archival evidence shows his actual political reach was limited.
• The damage was reputational: even Romanov relatives publicly condemned Alexandra’s reliance on him.
• Milyukov’s November 1916 ‘stupidity or treason’ speech listed Rasputin’s alleged influence as a key grievance, suggesting perception mattered more than reality.

Arguments that it is less convincing:
• Rasputin did secure some ministerial appointments, including Protopopov’s as Interior Minister in 1916.
• Yusupov’s decision to murder him suggests aristocrats took his influence seriously enough to act.
• Even if ‘modest’, his role was symptomatic of a court detached from political reality — arguably itself a real problem.

Secure: A clear evaluation supported by relevant detail on both sides.
Developing: An attempt to evaluate with limited contextual support.
Emerging: Description of the interpretation without independent evaluation.

lessons.title: The Provisional Government's Crisis
lessons.description: Dual Power, Order Number 1 and a government undone by war, land and bread.
lessons.content_html:
Two Authorities, Same Building

When Nicholas II abdicated on 2 March 1917 (Old Style), Russia had no obvious successor government. Two improvisations stepped into the gap. In one wing of the Tauride Palace, the Provisional Committee of the Duma announced itself as the Provisional Government, with the liberal landowner Prince Lvov as Prime Minister and Pavel Milyukov as Foreign Minister. The Kadet party dominated. In another wing, factory delegates and soldiers had reconstituted the soviet of 1905. The Petrograd Soviet’s Executive Committee, mostly Mensheviks and Socialist Revolutionaries, claimed to speak for the workers and the army. The arrangement was nicknamed Dual Power — two authorities in the same building, neither willing to overrule the other.

Key Fact

The Provisional Government formed in March 1917 was self-appointed from the old Duma; it was never elected and kept postponing the Constituent Assembly elections that would have given it a mandate. Its authority was permanently shared with the Petrograd Soviet under an unstable Dual Power arrangement.

Order Number 1

On 14 March (1 March, OS) the Petrograd Soviet issued Order Number 1 to the army. Soldiers were to elect committees that would control all weapons in their unit. They were to salute officers only on duty. They were to obey the Provisional Government only when its orders did not contradict those of the Soviet. The decree was meant to protect the revolution from a military coup. The unintended effect was to dissolve the discipline of the Russian army at the front, where soldiers immediately formed committees, refused to attack and began voting on whether to obey orders. Officers found themselves stripped of authority and, at the front, sometimes shot.

Continuing the War

The single greatest political question of 1917 was whether Russia should stay in the First World War. The Provisional Government, dominated by Kadets, said yes. They were liberals who believed Russia’s honour and Western alliances required victory; they also wanted the war aims of Tsarist diplomacy — control of Constantinople and the Straits. In April Milyukov sent a secret note to the Allies promising to fight until total victory. When it leaked, mass demonstrations broke out in Petrograd. Milyukov was forced to resign. Six socialists, including Alexander Kerensky, joined a coalition government in May. The change of personnel did not change the policy: Russia stayed in the war.

In June, Kerensky — now War Minister — launched a final offensive in Galicia to redeem Russian arms. The June Offensive collapsed within ten days. Whole units melted away; fraternisation with German troops became routine. By July half the Provisional Government’s authority over its own army had evaporated.

The Provisional Government’s second fatal hesitation was over land. The peasantry — 80% of the population — wanted noble estates broken up and redistributed. The Kadets believed this could only be done after the Constituent Assembly met, with full legal procedure and compensation for landlords. So they postponed it. Peasants did not wait. By the summer of 1917 they were seizing manor estates, burning records and dividing the land themselves. Soldiers at the front, hearing that their villages were getting land, began deserting in large numbers to claim their share. By October the front had effectively dissolved.

The July Days

In early July anti-government demonstrations in Petrograd, partly stoked by Bolshevik agitators, turned into something close to an armed uprising. The Bolsheviks were caught between encouraging a rising they did not feel ready for, and stepping back. Lenin appeared, hesitated, and then declined to take leadership. Loyal troops, brought in from the front, restored order. The Provisional Government published documents alleging that Lenin was a German agent (he had returned to Russia in April through Germany on a sealed train). Trotsky and other Bolshevik leaders were arrested. Lenin fled to Finland.

For about six weeks the Bolsheviks looked finished. By late August they would be back in business — rescued, paradoxically, by their enemies on the right.

The Kornilov Affair

Kerensky, who became Prime Minister in July, appointed General Lavr Kornilov as Commander-in-Chief in the hope of restoring military discipline. Kornilov, a tough Cossack soldier, believed the only solution was to crush the Petrograd Soviet entirely. In late August he ordered loyal troops to march on the capital. Whether Kerensky originally agreed and then panicked, or whether Kornilov acted on his own authority, remains disputed. What is clear is that on 27 August Kerensky publicly denounced Kornilov as a counter-revolutionary, dismissed him, and called on the Petrograd Soviet to defend the city.

The Soviet armed Bolshevik Red Guards from its arsenals; railway workers blocked Kornilov’s troop trains; agitators turned his soldiers against him. The march on Petrograd dissolved without a shot. Kornilov was arrested. Kerensky had defeated his own appointed commander. But the Bolsheviks emerged with weapons, prestige and a story to tell: only they had really stood up to counter-revolution. By September they had majorities in both the Petrograd and Moscow Soviets for the first time.

Bolshevik party membership grew from about 24,000 in April 1917 to perhaps 350,000 by October. Three things drove it. First, ‘Peace, Land, Bread’ said in three words what the Provisional Government would not say at all. Second, the soldiers’ committees set up by Order Number 1 became Bolshevik recruiting grounds once it was clear the war would continue. Third, the Kornilov Affair gave the party its breakthrough among workers and rank-and-file soldiers, who saw the Bolsheviks as the only force willing to fight counter-revolution. By September, factory workers in Petrograd were electing Bolshevik delegates; sailors at Kronstadt were already openly Bolshevik. Other socialist parties — Mensheviks, Socialist Revolutionaries — had all spent 1917 in coalition with the Provisional Government and were tarnished by its failures.

Key Fact

The Kornilov Affair of August 1917 was the political turning point of the year. By arming the Bolshevik Red Guards to defeat a perceived right-wing coup, Kerensky strengthened the very party that would overthrow him in October. Bolshevik membership of the Soviets had grown from a minority in July to a clear majority by September.

A Government with Nothing Left

By October 1917 the Provisional Government had no friends left. Liberals had been alienated by the leftward coalition; conservatives by Kerensky’s denunciation of Kornilov; soldiers by the failed June Offensive; peasants by the postponed land reform; workers by inflation and bread queues no different from those that had toppled Nicholas. The Constituent Assembly had been promised, postponed, then promised for November. The body that had stepped into the wreckage of the Romanov regime was now waiting, exhausted, for someone to push it over. The next chapter is about the small, disciplined party that did so.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For interpretation questions, recognise that liberal historians (Pipes, Lieven) tend to present the Provisional Government as the lost democratic alternative; revisionists (Fitzpatrick, Steinberg) tend to argue it was always undermined by its refusal to end the war or distribute land. The strongest answers test the interpretation against precise contextual knowledge: Milyukov’s April note, Order Number 1, the June Offensive, the Kornilov Affair. For chain-of-consequence questions, link July Days → Kornilov → Bolshevik recovery → October.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Provisional Government formed in March 1917 was self-appointed from the old Duma and shared authority with the Petrograd Soviet under an unstable Dual Power arrangement.
  • It failed to address the war (continuing it, then losing the June Offensive), land (postponing reform until the Constituent Assembly) or food shortages, all of which had brought down the Tsar.
  • The Kornilov Affair of August 1917 transformed the political situation: Kerensky armed the Bolsheviks to defeat the threat, and they emerged in September with majorities in the Petrograd and Moscow Soviets.

lessons.title: Lenin, Trotsky and the October Revolution
lessons.description: April Theses, the growth of the Bolsheviks and Red Guards storming the Winter Palace.
lessons.content_html:
A Sealed Train and a Slogan

When the Tsar fell in March 1917, Lenin was in Zürich. Cut off from Russia by the war, he reached the Finland Station in Petrograd on 3 April thanks to the German government, who paid for a sealed railway carriage to take him through Germany. They wanted Russia knocked out of the war; they expected Lenin to oblige. He delivered. The next morning he stunned even his own Bolshevik colleagues by reading out the April Theses: no cooperation with the Provisional Government; immediate end to the war; all power to the soviets; nationalisation of land; the slogan ‘Peace, Land, Bread’.

Key Fact

Lenin’s slogan ‘Peace, Land, Bread’ was the political masterstroke of 1917. ‘Peace’ appealed to soldiers and to war-weary cities; ‘Land’ appealed to peasants who wanted the noble estates broken up; ‘Bread’ appealed to workers facing inflation and food queues. No other party offered all three.

Trotsky Joins

Lenin’s most important new ally was Leon Trotsky, who returned to Petrograd from New York in May. Trotsky had spent fifteen years as an independent Marxist outside both factions of the Mensheviks and Bolsheviks; he had been close to the former at the 1903 split. Now he formally joined the Bolsheviks. He was arguably their best public speaker, a battle-hardened veteran of the 1905 St Petersburg Soviet, and a brilliant organiser. With Lenin in hiding for parts of the year and other senior Bolsheviks (Stalin, Kamenev, Zinoviev) more cautious, Trotsky’s combination of theory, oratory and military instinct would matter decisively.

A Disciplined Party

The Bolsheviks were not large in 1917. In April they had perhaps 24,000 members; by October maybe 350,000. What made them effective was not size but discipline. Lenin’s 1903 demand for a small party of professional revolutionaries had produced a body where the central committee’s decisions were binding on every cell. Their newspaper Pravda repeated the same slogans week after week. Their agitators were trained to give the same answers to the same questions in any factory or barracks. While other socialist groups debated, the Bolsheviks acted.

After the Kornilov Affair in August 1917 (covered in the previous lesson), the Bolsheviks emerged with arms, prestige, and growing soviet majorities. By 25 September they controlled the Petrograd Soviet under Trotsky as chairman. By early October Lenin, still hiding in Finland, was writing letters to the central committee demanding immediate insurrection.

On 10 October (OS) the Bolshevik central committee met in secret in Petrograd. Lenin had returned in disguise. He demanded an immediate seizure of power before the Constituent Assembly elections, which he expected the Bolsheviks to lose. Two senior Bolsheviks — Kamenev and Zinoviev — opposed insurrection and were so worried they leaked the plan to the press. Most of the committee voted with Lenin. Practical preparation was handed to Trotsky’s newly created Military Revolutionary Committee of the Petrograd Soviet, which would coordinate the seizure under the cover of defending the Soviet from a supposed government coup.

The October Insurrection

The seizure of power began on the night of 24–25 October (6–7 November, NS). Sailors from the Kronstadt naval base, Bolshevik Red Guards from the factories and pro-Bolshevik units of the Petrograd garrison occupied the central railway stations, telegraph office, post office, state bank and bridges. Resistance was minimal; many Provisional Government supporters had already fled or simply refused to fight. Kerensky escaped Petrograd that morning to look for loyal troops, leaving his cabinet to be arrested in the Winter Palace.

The Winter Palace fell in the early hours of 26 October. The cruiser Aurora fired blank shells from the Neva to signal the assault. Inside, the cabinet was guarded by a few hundred officer cadets and the Women’s Battalion of Death; resistance was brief and casualties light. Soviet propaganda would later film a stylised ‘storming’, but in reality the takeover was closer to a tightly organised coup than a popular uprising.

As the Winter Palace fell, the Second All-Russian Congress of Soviets opened in the Smolny Institute. The Bolsheviks held a narrow majority. Mensheviks and right-wing Socialist Revolutionaries walked out in protest at the seizure of power, leaving the floor to Lenin’s party and the Left Socialist Revolutionaries. Trotsky famously dismissed the departing Mensheviks: ‘You are pitiful isolated individuals; you are bankrupts; your role is played out. Go where you belong from now on — into the dustbin of history!’ The Congress passed the Decree on Peace (calling for an immediate end to the war) and the Decree on Land (abolishing private ownership). A new government — the Council of People’s Commissars (Sovnarkom) — was named, with Lenin as chairman.

Why the Bolsheviks Won in 1917

The Bolshevik victory was not predetermined. It came from the combination of two long-running weaknesses in their opponents and three Bolshevik strengths. Their opponents’ weaknesses: the Provisional Government refused to end the war or distribute land, and Dual Power meant it could not coerce its own population. Their strengths: a clear, popular slogan that no rival could match; a tightly disciplined party that could act when others debated; and Trotsky’s organisational skill in turning the Petrograd Soviet’s Military Revolutionary Committee into the instrument of the seizure.

It is fashionable to argue that the Bolsheviks were lucky — that in any of a dozen moments between April and October the situation could have gone the other way. That is true. It is also true that they were the only party who had organised themselves to take advantage of luck when it came.

Key Fact

The October Revolution was a tightly planned coup, not a mass uprising. Trotsky’s Military Revolutionary Committee coordinated armed workers, sailors and pro-Bolshevik soldiers to seize key buildings on the night of 24–25 October. The Winter Palace fell in the early hours of 26 October with light casualties. The Second Congress of Soviets ratified the new government the next morning.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For interpretations of October, contrast the totalitarian school (Pipes, Conquest) which presents the seizure as a coup imposed by a fanatical minority with the revisionist tradition (Fitzpatrick) which stresses how the Bolsheviks rode a real wave of soldier and worker discontent. Strong answers to chain-of-consequence questions trace April Theses → July Days setback → Kornilov rescue → Soviet majority → 10 October vote → seizure. Avoid first-person voice in essays — you cannot reach the AO2 analytical descriptors that way.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Lenin’s April Theses and the slogan ‘Peace, Land, Bread’ gave the Bolsheviks a clear, popular programme that no rival party could match.
  • Bolshevik organisational discipline, combined with Trotsky’s recruitment in May 1917 and the political opening created by the Kornilov Affair in August, transformed the party from a weak minority into the strongest force in the Petrograd Soviet by September.
  • The October seizure of power on 24–26 October 1917 was a tightly planned coup, not a mass uprising; the Second Congress of Soviets ratified the Bolshevik government the next morning under Lenin as chairman of Sovnarkom.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A is from the British historian Robert Service (Lenin: A Biography, 2000), arguing that the October Revolution succeeded mainly because of Lenin’s own ruthless determination to seize power against his colleagues’ caution. Interpretation B is from the British historian Orlando Figes (A People’s Tragedy, 1996), arguing that October succeeded because the Provisional Government had already destroyed itself.
Identify two ways in which the interpretations of October 1917 differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Service emphasises Lenin’s personal will; Figes emphasises the structural collapse of the Provisional Government.
• Service treats October as a Bolshevik achievement; Figes treats it as a default outcome.
• Service focuses on intra-party debate (Lenin vs Kamenev/Zinoviev); Figes focuses on the wider political context.

Mastering: Two precise differences identified with reference to both interpretations.
Secure: Two clear differences with grounding in both.
Developing: One clear difference plus a vague second point.
Emerging: General comments without specific differences.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why these two interpretations of October 1917 differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• Different evidence: Service uses Lenin’s letters and central committee minutes; Figes uses social history of soldiers, peasants and workers.
• Different purposes: Service is writing a biography of Lenin and naturally foregrounds the man; Figes is writing a panoramic narrative of the revolution.
• Different perspectives: Service focuses on agency; Figes focuses on context.
• Different time of writing: both are post-Soviet, but Figes’s panoramic approach reflects the new social-history wave of the 1990s.

Mastering: A clear reason explained with specific support.
Secure: A clear reason with reference to both interpretations.
Developing: A reason identified but not fully developed.
Emerging: General comment without explanation.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A claims that ‘the October Revolution was a tightly planned coup by a few thousand armed men, not a mass popular rising.’
How convincing is this interpretation? Use Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge to evaluate.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Arguments that the interpretation is convincing:
• Trotsky’s Military Revolutionary Committee coordinated the seizure of stations, bridges and government buildings using a few thousand Red Guards, sailors and soldiers.
• Casualties at the Winter Palace were light; defenders were a few hundred cadets and the Women’s Battalion.
• Most Petrograd citizens slept through the night and woke up to find a new government.

Arguments that it is less convincing:
• The Bolsheviks held a majority in the Petrograd and Moscow Soviets by September, suggesting genuine mass support among workers and soldiers.
• The Second Congress of Soviets ratified the takeover the next morning, giving it a degree of popular legitimacy.
• A coup cannot succeed without an underlying political climate ready to accept it — mass disillusionment with the Provisional Government was real.

Mastering: A substantiated evaluation testing the interpretation against precise contextual knowledge.
Secure: A clear evaluation with relevant detail on both sides.
Developing: An attempt to evaluate with limited contextual support.
Emerging: Description of the interpretation without independent evaluation.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Lenin’s April Theses on Bolshevik strategy in 1917.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Students may include:
• They reversed the Bolshevik leadership’s previous willingness to cooperate with the Provisional Government; Stalin and Kamenev had been arguing for conditional support before April.
• They produced the slogan ‘Peace, Land, Bread’, which separated the Bolsheviks from every other socialist group.
• They committed the party to ending the war, gaining soldier support that culminated in the September soviet majorities.
• They argued for ‘all power to the soviets’, providing the institutional cover under which October would be presented.
• They set the framework for the eventual rejection of the Constituent Assembly in January 1918.

Mastering: A chain of consequences linking the April Theses to October.
Secure: Two or more developed effects with specific support.
Developing: One developed effect; others mentioned briefly.
Emerging: General comments about Lenin.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘The Bolsheviks won power in October 1917 mainly because of the strength of their party organisation.’
How far do you accept this view? In your answer you should:
• consider the strengths of Bolshevik organisation
• consider other factors (such as the failures of the Provisional Government and the Kornilov Affair)
• reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark scheme guidance:
Arguments for organisation being the most important factor:
• Lenin’s 1903 model produced a disciplined party able to act decisively on 24–25 October.
• Trotsky’s Military Revolutionary Committee was a precise instrument other socialist groups could not match.
• Membership grew from 24,000 in April to 350,000 by October — the apparatus could mobilise.

Arguments for other factors:
• The Provisional Government’s refusal to end the war or distribute land created the political conditions for Bolshevik growth.
• The Kornilov Affair handed the Bolsheviks weapons, prestige and Soviet majorities.
• Lenin’s personal insistence on immediate insurrection was decisive against Kamenev and Zinoviev.

Judgement should weigh agency (party, leader) against context (war, land, Kornilov).

Mastering: Substantiated judgement weighing factors with precise evidence.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence.
Developing: Description with limited weighing.
Emerging: Narrative on one factor only.
