lessons.title: Lenin in Power: Brest-Litovsk, Cheka and Civil War
lessons.description: Lenin's first decrees, the harsh peace at Brest-Litovsk, the Cheka, and the Civil War.
lessons.content_html:
When the Bolsheviks seized power in October 1917 they controlled little beyond Petrograd and Moscow. Within four years they had ended Russia’s war with Germany, dispersed an elected assembly, fought a brutal civil war and built a one-party state. The tools they used — rapid decrees, a feared secret police and Trotsky’s Red Army — defined the new regime.

First Decrees and the Constituent Assembly

Within days of the October Revolution, Lenin issued sweeping decrees to win popular support. The Decree on Land legalised peasants seizing landlord estates. The Decree on Peace called for an immediate end to the First World War without annexations. The Decree on Workers’ Control gave factory committees authority over their workplaces. Banks, railways and large industries were nationalised in the weeks that followed.

Elections to the long-promised Constituent Assembly were held in November 1917. The Bolsheviks came second, winning under a quarter of the seats; the Socialist Revolutionaries (SRs), with their rural base, came first. When the Assembly met in Petrograd in January 1918, Lenin allowed it to sit for one day before Red Guards closed the building. The Bolsheviks ruled instead through the Soviets — bodies they could dominate.

Key Fact

Lenin secured early support with three decrees — Land (peasants keep the estates they took), Peace (end the war) and Workers’ Control (factory committees run industry). The dispersal of the elected Constituent Assembly in January 1918 showed the regime would not share power.

The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, March 1918

Honouring the Decree on Peace meant doing a deal with Germany. Trotsky led the Soviet delegation and tried delaying tactics, but a renewed German advance forced acceptance. The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk stripped Russia of Ukraine, Poland, Finland, the Baltic provinces and parts of the Caucasus — roughly a third of the population, half of industry and most of its coal.

Lenin defended the treaty as a tactical retreat: peace bought time to consolidate the revolution at home. Critics argued it betrayed the international socialist cause and handed away the country’s industrial heartland. The treaty was annulled when Germany surrendered to the Western Allies eight months later, but the political damage in Russia had been done. Anti-Bolshevik forces accused Lenin of being a German agent and used Brest-Litovsk to justify the coming Civil War.

The Cheka and the Red Terror

In December 1917 Lenin set up the Cheka, the All-Russian Extraordinary Commission, under Felix Dzerzhinsky. Its job was to root out ‘counter-revolution and sabotage’ without trial. After an SR activist shot and wounded Lenin in August 1918, the Cheka launched the official Red Terror — mass arrests, summary executions and hostage-taking in cities across Soviet-held Russia. By 1922 the Cheka had executed an estimated 140,000 people.

The Cheka of 1917-22 should not be confused with the NKVD that Stalin used in the 1930s — they were different organisations from different decades. The Cheka was renamed the GPU in 1922; later reorganisations eventually produced the NKVD. The continuity was the institutional acceptance of secret-police violence as a tool of government, but the Red Terror under Lenin was justified as a wartime emergency measure rather than a permanent feature of peacetime rule.

Nicholas II, his wife Alexandra, their five children and four servants were shot in a cellar in Ekaterinburg on the night of 16-17 July 1918, as White forces approached the city. The local Bolsheviks acted with Moscow’s authorisation. The killing closed off any restoration of the dynasty and signalled that the regime would not allow a rallying point to survive. The bodies were hidden until the 1990s, when DNA testing confirmed the family’s identification and they were reburied in St Petersburg in 1998.

The Civil War, 1918-1921

War broke out across the former empire. The Bolsheviks (Reds) faced the Whites — a loose collection of monarchists, liberals, ex-Tsarist officers and Socialist Revolutionaries — supported at points by Britain, France, the USA and Japan. Peasant Green armies fought both sides. White generals included Anton Denikin in the south, Alexander Kolchak in Siberia, Nikolai Yudenich near Petrograd and Pyotr Wrangel in Crimea.

The Whites were never a single army. Denikin and Kolchak operated thousands of miles apart and never coordinated a joint offensive. Their political programmes ranged from restoring the Tsar to convening a constitutional assembly — an inconsistency that alienated peasants who feared the return of landlords.

Geography: the Reds held the central core — Moscow, Petrograd, the railway hubs and most of the population. They could shift troops along interior lines while the Whites had to coordinate around the rim. Leadership: Trotsky as War Commissar built the Red Army from a few thousand Red Guards into a force of five million by 1920, using ex-Tsarist officers under political commissars. Unity: the Bolsheviks had a single command and a clear cause — defending the revolution. Propaganda: posters, agit-trains and films cast the Whites as agents of foreign capital, while rural Russia feared a White victory would reverse the land seizures of 1917.

Key Fact

The Reds won the Civil War because they held the central core with its railways and people, faced divided enemies who never coordinated, had Trotsky’s disciplined Red Army with ex-Tsarist officers under commissar control, and used propaganda to frame the conflict as defence of land redistribution against a foreign-backed restoration.

By 1921 the Whites had been driven out, but Soviet Russia was wrecked. Industrial output had collapsed, millions had died from fighting, disease and famine, and a third of the population had been ruled briefly by White or foreign forces. The Bolshevik Party had survived — but only by transforming itself into a militarised state run from Moscow with a secret police, a mass army and no remaining political opposition.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Explain Effects question on Brest-Litovsk or the Civil War, build a chain of consequences rather than listing changes. Brest-Litovsk → territorial loss → White anger → Civil War → Red Terror works far better than ‘Russia lost Ukraine, then there was a war, then the Cheka killed people’. For 12-mark Period Essays comparing two factors (e.g. Trotsky’s leadership versus White divisions in the Red victory), reach an explicit overall judgement — examiner reports flag the missing judgement step every series.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Lenin’s early decrees on Land, Peace and Workers’ Control bought support, but dispersing the Constituent Assembly in January 1918 showed the regime was a one-party dictatorship from the start.
  • The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk ended the war on humiliating terms but freed Lenin to focus on internal enemies; the Cheka under Dzerzhinsky and the Red Terror after August 1918 institutionalised secret-police violence.
  • The Reds won the Civil War through interior lines, unity of command, Trotsky’s Red Army of five million and a peasant fear that a White victory would mean losing the land — not because the Whites lacked soldiers.

practice_questions.text: How does Interpretation A differ in tone from Interpretation B about the early Soviet government? Use Interpretations A and B to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A treats Lenin’s early decrees as popular, practical responses to peasant land hunger and war weariness; B treats them as cynical promises designed to neutralise opponents until the Cheka could be built.
• A presents the dispersal of the Constituent Assembly as a regrettable necessity; B presents it as proof the Bolsheviks never intended to share power.
• Reference must be made to specific content of both interpretations rather than just paraphrase.
[4 marks — Mastering: clear comparison of tone with precise textual evidence from both interpretations. Secure: comparison made with some textual reference. Developing: paraphrase of each rather than comparison. Emerging: one interpretation only.]

practice_questions.text: Why might Interpretations A and B give different views about the role of the Cheka under Lenin?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Different purposes: A may be a Soviet-era textbook defending the Cheka as a wartime necessity; B may be a Western academic study highlighting Red Terror victims.
• Different time of writing: post-1991 access to Cheka archives changed what historians could say.
• Different perspectives or schools: orthodox Soviet versus liberal/Western (e.g. Pipes) framings of Bolshevik violence.
• Different evidence base — memoirs, party records, victim testimony.
[4 marks — Mastering: explains two distinct reasons rooted in purpose, evidence, time of writing or perspective. Secure: one developed reason and one undeveloped. Developing: identifies a reason without explanation. Emerging: describes what the interpretations say rather than why they differ.]

practice_questions.text: How convincing is Interpretation A about the reasons the Bolsheviks won the Civil War? Use Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Test what the interpretation claims (e.g. that Trotsky’s leadership was decisive) against named contextual evidence: Trotsky’s armoured train, use of ex-Tsarist officers under commissars, Red Army growth from c.300,000 to c.5 million.
• Weigh against alternative factors: White disunity (Denikin and Kolchak never coordinating), Red interior lines around Moscow and Petrograd, peasant fear of landlord restoration.
• Note historiographical position — totalitarian-school readings emphasise Bolshevik organisation; revisionists stress structural advantages.
• Reach a substantiated judgement on how convincing the interpretation is overall.
[8 marks — Mastering: precise contextual knowledge tests the interpretation and reaches a substantiated judgement. Secure: relevant knowledge applied with a clear judgement. Developing: knowledge used but unevenly linked. Emerging: describes the interpretation without testing it.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk on Russia in 1918.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Territorial: loss of Ukraine, Poland, Finland, the Baltic provinces — about a third of the population and half of industry.
• Economic: loss of coal and grain regions worsened food shortages and contributed to War Communism.
• Political: the treaty split the Bolsheviks from the Left SRs, prompting the SR uprising and the August 1918 attempt on Lenin’s life.
• Military: White generals used the treaty to recruit support, accelerating the Civil War.
• Effects must be linked in chains rather than listed.
[8 marks — Mastering: chains of consequence with precise detail. Secure: clear effects with some development. Developing: effects identified but undeveloped. Emerging: simple description of the treaty.]

practice_questions.text: ‘Trotsky’s leadership of the Red Army was the most important reason the Bolsheviks won the Civil War.’ Evaluate this view. You should consider Trotsky’s leadership, White disunity and other relevant factors, and reach a substantiated judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments for Trotsky’s leadership being most important:
• Built Red Army from c.300,000 to c.5 million using ex-Tsarist officers under political commissars.
• Personally directed front-line operations from his armoured train; held Petrograd against Yudenich.
• Imposed iron discipline including the death penalty for desertion.

Arguments for other factors:
• Geography: Reds held the centre with the railway network; could move troops on interior lines.
• White disunity: Denikin, Kolchak, Yudenich and Wrangel never coordinated; political aims clashed.
• Peasant attitudes: fear that a White victory would reverse the 1917 land seizures.
• Foreign intervention was small in scale and gave the Bolsheviks a propaganda gift.

lessons.title: War Communism, Kronstadt and the NEP
lessons.description: War Communism, the Kronstadt sailors’ revolt and Lenin’s tactical retreat to the NEP.
lessons.content_html:
The Civil War left the Soviet economy in collapse. Industrial output stood at a fifth of pre-war levels, the cities had emptied as workers fled to the countryside in search of food, and a famine in 1921-22 killed perhaps five million people. The policy that fed the Red Army — War Communism — held the regime together but produced famine, peasant revolts and finally an uprising of Kronstadt sailors who had once been the ‘pride of the revolution’.

War Communism, 1918-1921

War Communism was a set of emergency measures designed to win the Civil War, not a planned economy. The state nationalised all industry above the smallest workshops. Private trade was outlawed; the few who broke the rules were called ‘bagmen’ and shot. Workers were drafted into labour battalions and paid in rations. The most damaging element was grain requisitioning — armed detachments seized peasants’ harvests at fixed low prices, often taking the seed grain too.

Predictably, peasants stopped growing surplus grain. Why grow what would only be confiscated? Sown area shrank year on year. Combined with civil-war disruption and the loss of Ukraine’s grain belt under Brest-Litovsk, this triggered a catastrophic famine in the Volga region in 1921-22. The Bolsheviks, who had banned all private charity, eventually accepted aid from Herbert Hoover’s American Relief Administration to keep millions alive.

Key Fact

War Communism (1918-21) used grain requisitioning, banned private trade, and militarised labour to keep the Red Army fed. The cost was a collapsed economy and the Volga famine of 1921-22, which killed roughly five million people.

The Tambov Rising and Rural Revolt

By 1920 peasant rebellions covered large parts of European Russia. The most serious was the Tambov Rising under Alexander Antonov, where some 50,000 armed peasants defied the regime for over a year. Lenin sent the Red Army with chemical weapons and concentration camps for hostage families. The countryside was being reconquered.

The Kronstadt Rising, March 1921

The shock came from a different direction. The sailors of the Kronstadt naval base, just outside Petrograd, had been Bolshevik heroes in 1917. Trotsky had called them the ‘pride and glory of the Russian revolution’. In March 1921 they issued fifteen demands: free elections to the Soviets, freedom of speech for socialist parties, freedom of trade unions, an end to grain requisitioning, and the release of socialist political prisoners.

It was these demands — from revolutionary insiders, not Tsarist enemies — that frightened Lenin most. He branded the Kronstadters as White-led mutineers. Trotsky ordered the Red Army across the frozen ice to storm the fortress. Several thousand sailors were killed; many more were arrested and shot in the weeks afterwards. The rising was crushed, but the message had reached Moscow: the regime’s own base was in revolt against War Communism.

The Tenth Party Congress met in Moscow as Kronstadt was being crushed. It made two huge decisions. First, it announced the New Economic Policy, replacing requisitioning with a tax in kind. Second, it banned factions inside the party — the Workers’ Opposition led by Alexandra Kollontai and Alexander Shlyapnikov, which had argued for more trade-union power, was outlawed. The price of economic relaxation was tighter political control. From 1921 on, dissent was channelled inside one party, and that party would not allow internal disagreement to surface.

The New Economic Policy, 1921

The New Economic Policy (NEP) replaced grain requisitioning with a tax in kind: peasants paid a fixed percentage of their crop and could sell the surplus. Small private workshops and shops were legalised. Foreign concessions were granted to bring in capital. The state kept the ‘commanding heights’ — heavy industry, banking, foreign trade, transport — but the rest reverted to a market.

The economic results were rapid. By 1926 industrial and agricultural output had recovered to roughly 1913 levels. Peasants planted more, queued less. A new class of small traders, the ‘Nepmen’, ran shops in the cities. Hardliners called the NEP a betrayal of socialism — the worst Bolshevik insult was to be called a ‘NEP-man’.

Lenin defended the NEP as a temporary retreat — ‘one step backwards, two steps forward’. The political dictatorship of the party was reinforced even as economic life relaxed. Bukharin embraced it and argued it should run for ‘decades’. Left critics, including Trotsky, warned it was empowering rural capitalists and small traders at socialism’s expense. The unresolved tension — abandon the NEP and force industrialisation, or extend it and accept slower growth — became the central question of the post-Lenin power struggle.

Key Fact

The chain runs Kronstadt → Tenth Party Congress → NEP. The sailors’ revolt convinced Lenin that War Communism could not survive peace; the same Congress that crushed Kronstadt also abandoned grain requisitioning and banned factions, trading economic relaxation for tighter party control.

Lenin’s Achievements by 1924

When Lenin died in January 1924, the Soviet state had survived a civil war, ended a famine, and recovered roughly to 1913 economic levels. The political settlement, however, was a one-party dictatorship with a militarised secret police and no permitted opposition either outside or inside the party. Trotsky as War Commissar had built the Red Army that won the war; Lenin’s tactical flexibility had produced both War Communism and the NEP. The price had been paid in lives, principles and political pluralism.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The chain War Communism → famine → Kronstadt → NEP is a gold-standard answer to an 8-mark Explain Effects question. Examiner reports praise students who show consequences flowing into each other rather than listing ‘there was famine, then there was Kronstadt, then there was NEP’. For 8-mark Evaluate an Interpretation questions, contrast the totalitarian-school reading (NEP as cynical retreat by an authoritarian leader) with revisionist accounts that stress how widely Bolshevik insiders supported the change.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • War Communism (1918-21) won the Civil War but produced famine in 1921-22 (about five million dead) and triggered widespread peasant and worker revolt.
  • The Kronstadt Rising of March 1921 was crushed by Trotsky’s Red Army but proved that even Bolshevik insiders rejected War Communism.
  • The Tenth Party Congress launched the NEP — tax in kind plus legalised small trade — while banning factions; economic relaxation came with tighter political control.

lessons.title: The Power Struggle to Succeed Lenin
lessons.description: How Stalin outmanoeuvred Trotsky, Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin to succeed Lenin.
lessons.content_html:
When Lenin died in January 1924, no one believed Joseph Stalin would replace him. The Bolshevik leadership treated him as a dull bureaucrat — a ‘grey blur’ in Sukhanov’s phrase. Five years later he had isolated and defeated every rival. The struggle was won not at mass rallies but inside party committees, through control of appointments and the suppression of Lenin’s last warnings.

Lenin’s Death and Suppressed Testament

Lenin had a series of strokes from May 1922 and died on 21 January 1924. Before he became fully incapacitated, he dictated a document that became known as Lenin’s Testament. It assessed each of the leading Bolsheviks. Trotsky was ‘the most able man in the present Central Committee’ but ‘too self-confident’. Stalin was ‘too rude’, had ‘concentrated unlimited authority’ in his hands as General Secretary, and should be removed from the post.

Trotsky chose not to fight on the Testament. Zinoviev and Kamenev, who at that point saw Trotsky as the bigger threat, agreed with Stalin to suppress the document at the Thirteenth Party Congress in May 1924. The party rank and file never read it. Stalin survived a moment that could have ended his career.

Key Fact

In May 1924, Zinoviev and Kamenev sided with Stalin to suppress Lenin’s Testament because they feared Trotsky more. The decision saved Stalin’s career and shows that the power struggle was decided by tactical alliances among rivals, not Lenin’s wishes.

The Contenders

By 1924 there were five plausible heirs:

  • Leon Trotsky — founder of the Red Army, brilliant orator, intellectual force of the revolution. Many in 1924 expected him to inherit. His Jewish background, late conversion to Bolshevism (1917), and reputation for arrogance worked against him.
  • Joseph Stalin — General Secretary from April 1922. Controlled who got into the party, who chaired local committees, who sat at congresses. Often dismissed as a ‘mediocrity’.
  • Grigori Zinoviev — head of the Petrograd party and the Comintern.
  • Lev Kamenev — head of the Moscow party and Lenin’s former editor.
  • Nikolai Bukharin — the party’s leading economist and editor of Pravda; main intellectual defender of the NEP.

Stalin lacked the obvious assets of his rivals. He was not a brilliant theorist like Bukharin, a great orator like Trotsky or a famous revolutionary leader like Zinoviev. He spoke Russian with a heavy Georgian accent and rarely engaged in the polished debate culture of the Moscow intelligentsia. To Bolshevik insiders he looked like a competent administrator at best. The Menshevik writer Sukhanov dismissed him as ‘a grey blur’. The underestimation was strategic luck for Stalin: while his rivals fought each other in the limelight, he quietly built the network of appointments that decided Politburo and Congress votes. By the time the others realised the danger, the levers had already changed hands.

Permanent Revolution vs Socialism in One Country

The succession was fought partly through ideology. Trotsky argued for Permanent Revolution — that Soviet Russia could not survive long term unless revolution spread internationally. With Western workers’ movements failing in the early 1920s, this position looked increasingly bleak.

Stalin offered the alternative of Socialism in One Country. The USSR, Stalin claimed, could build socialism inside its own borders. The argument flattered Russian patriotism, fitted the mood of a country exhausted by world war, and let exhausted Bolsheviks focus on practical problems at home. Stalin’s slogan won the argument among the rank and file even before it won the Politburo.

The Triumvirate Against Trotsky, 1924-1925

From 1924 to 1925, Stalin, Zinoviev and Kamenev formed a triumvirate against Trotsky. Trotsky published *Lessons of October* (1924), accusing Zinoviev and Kamenev of opposing the October Revolution; they replied by accusing him of underestimating the peasantry. Stalin stayed largely above the fight, presenting himself as the moderate centre. By January 1925 Trotsky was forced to resign as War Commissar — the last lever he had on the Red Army was gone.

As General Secretary, Stalin controlled the appointment of party officials at every level — gorkom secretaries, factory cell chairs, provincial committee chairs. By the time of the Fourteenth Party Congress in 1925, the delegates had largely been put there by Stalin’s machine. The Lenin Enrolment of 1924 brought in roughly 240,000 new members, mostly chosen with Stalin’s approval. They were loyal not to Trotsky’s reputation but to the men who promoted them. Trotsky later wrote: ‘Stalin did not create the apparatus. The apparatus created Stalin.’

The United Opposition and the Right, 1925-1929

In 1925 Stalin turned on his triumvirate partners. Allying with Bukharin, Stalin attacked Zinoviev and Kamenev for ‘underestimating the peasantry’. They lost their Petrograd and Moscow bases. In a panic they joined Trotsky to form the ‘United Opposition’ in 1926, calling for faster industrialisation and an end to the NEP. Stalin’s control of the apparatus crushed them: in November 1927 they were expelled from the party. Trotsky was exiled to Alma-Ata in January 1928, then deported from the USSR in 1929.

With Trotsky gone, Stalin then turned on Bukharin and the ‘Right Deviation’. Stalin abandoned the NEP for forced collectivisation, calling Bukharin’s defence of peasant prosperity a betrayal. Bukharin was removed from Pravda and the Politburo by November 1929. By the end of that year, no rival remained at the top of the party. Stalin had taken five years to do what Lenin’s Testament had warned could happen if he was not removed.

Key Fact

Stalin’s sequence was tactical: ally with Zinoviev and Kamenev to crush Trotsky (1924-25), then ally with Bukharin to crush Zinoviev and Kamenev (1925-27), then turn on Bukharin (1928-29). Each rival helped destroy the next group before being destroyed in turn.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 12-mark Period Essays on the power struggle, the highest band requires a substantiated overall judgement — e.g. ‘Stalin’s control of party appointments mattered more than ideology because it gave him the votes before the policy debates began.’ Don’t just cover Trotsky vs Stalin in turn. For 8-mark Evaluate an Interpretation, totalitarian readings (Stalin as inevitable winner through ruthlessness) clash with revisionist views (rivals destroyed themselves through tactical mistakes) — name the school of thought to access top marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Lenin’s Testament called for Stalin’s removal but was suppressed by Zinoviev and Kamenev in 1924, who feared Trotsky more — Stalin’s most dangerous moment.
  • Stalin’s position as General Secretary from 1922 gave him control of party appointments — the bureaucratic foundation of victory.
  • Stalin defeated his rivals in sequence (Trotsky 1924-29, Zinoviev/Kamenev 1925-27, Bukharin 1928-29) by switching alliances and adopting his opponents’ policies once they were defeated.

lessons.title: Collectivisation and the War on the Kulaks
lessons.description: Forced grain seizures, dekulakisation and the catastrophic Ukrainian famine of 1932-33.
lessons.content_html:
In 1928 Stalin abandoned the NEP. The Five Year Plans needed grain to feed the cities and to export for foreign currency, and the peasants were not delivering enough. Stalin’s solution was to take farming out of peasant hands altogether. The result, between 1929 and 1933, was the most violent transformation of rural Europe in modern history: an estimated five to seven million dead, a famine that ravaged Ukraine and Kazakhstan, and the destruction of an entire way of life.

The ‘Great Turn’ of 1928

By 1927 a ‘grain procurement crisis’ meant the state was buying about 25 per cent less grain than the year before. Bukharin argued for higher prices and continued NEP. Stalin instead drove a hard line: peasants were hoarding grain, and the Five Year Plans could not wait. The Great Turn of 1928 ended the NEP and committed the state to forced industrialisation paid for by squeezing the countryside.

How Collectivisation Worked

Collectivisation meant peasants surrendered their land, livestock and tools to a collective. Two structures dominated:

  • The kolkhoz: a notionally cooperative collective farm. Peasants worked the land together; the state took a fixed quota first, then peasants were paid in kind from what remained. They kept tiny private plots.
  • The sovkhoz: a state farm where peasants were paid wages like factory workers; less common but more directly state-run.

Tractors, ploughs and other machinery were concentrated in Machine Tractor Stations (MTS), which hired equipment to the kolkhozes for a fee paid in grain. Each MTS had a political department that watched the surrounding farms. The state could reach into rural Russia in a way the Tsars never had.

Key Fact

Collectivisation merged peasant farms into kolkhozes (cooperative collectives) and sovkhozes (state farms). Machine Tractor Stations supplied equipment and political surveillance, giving the state direct control of grain extraction.

Dekulakisation

In December 1929 Stalin called for ‘the liquidation of the kulaks as a class’. The kulak label, which had once meant a richer peasant employing labour, was now applied to almost anyone resisting collectivisation. A peasant with one extra cow, two horses, or a metal roof could be denounced. Roughly a fifth of dekulakised families were executed or sent to forced-labour colonies; another two thirds were deported to Siberia, the Urals or Kazakhstan. Over five million people were affected.

The label was politically constructed. Local activists faced quotas: each district had to find its kulaks. As one historian put it, the dekulakisation campaign was less a war on rich peasants than a quota-driven assault on the most successful tenth of the village.

Peasants resisted in ways open to the powerless. Many slaughtered their livestock rather than hand it over: between 1929 and 1933, USSR cattle stocks fell from about 70 million head to 38 million, sheep and goats from 147 million to 50 million, horses from 33 million to 16 million. Peasants buried grain, broke tools, or fled to the cities. Stalin briefly retreated in March 1930 with his article ‘Dizzy with Success’, blaming over-zealous local officials for ‘excesses’ — but the policy resumed within months.

The Famine of 1932-1933

By 1932 sown area had collapsed and grain output was below 1928 levels — yet state procurement quotas were raised, partly to fund industrial imports. The collision produced famine. The hardest-hit areas were Ukraine, the North Caucasus and Kazakhstan. In Ukraine, where the famine is now called the Holodomor (‘death by hunger’), about four million people died. In Kazakhstan, around 1.5 million Kazakhs — nearly a quarter of the population — died as nomadic herding was destroyed and forced settlement disrupted the seasonal grazing on which Kazakh life depended.

Soviet authorities denied the famine externally and prevented peasants from leaving the affected regions through internal passport controls (introduced December 1932). The Soviet press carried no reports; foreign journalists in Moscow who tried to investigate, such as the Welshman Gareth Jones, were dismissed and discredited by colleagues. Survivors described eating bark, weeds, leather and, in extreme cases, human corpses. Whether Stalin deliberately engineered the Ukrainian famine to crush Ukrainian national identity, or whether it was a product of brutal policy without specific genocidal intent, remains debated. Many historians, the Ukrainian state and several governments now classify the Holodomor as genocide; Russian and some Western historians question the deliberate-targeting argument while accepting Stalin’s responsibility for mass death.

In political terms, yes — the state could now extract grain at will, fund industrial imports, and control the countryside. By 1936, around 90 per cent of peasants worked on collective farms. In agricultural terms, no — Soviet grain output did not regain 1928 levels for decades. Livestock numbers took even longer to recover. Examiner reports flag students who write ‘collectivisation succeeded’ without distinguishing between political control (the regime won) and productivity (the regime lost).

Key Fact

The 1932-33 famine killed roughly four million Ukrainians (the Holodomor) and around 1.5 million Kazakhs. Causes included raised grain quotas, peasant resistance through livestock slaughter, and internal passports introduced in December 1932 that prevented escape from famine zones.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Examiner reports repeatedly flag the ‘all kulaks were rich’ misconception — demonstrate you know the label was applied loosely. For 8-mark Explain Effects on collectivisation, build the chain end-of-NEP → quotas → resistance → livestock slaughter → famine → political control rather than listing changes. For 8-mark Evaluate an Interpretation, contrast totalitarian readings (Stalin engineered the famine) with revisionist accounts (chaotic policy with disastrous results) — and reach a substantiated judgement.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Stalin’s ‘Great Turn’ of 1928 ended the NEP and committed the regime to forced collectivisation: kolkhozes, sovkhozes and Machine Tractor Stations replaced the peasant village.
  • Dekulakisation affected over five million people; the kulak label was applied loosely to anyone resisting, and a fifth of those targeted were executed or worked to death.
  • The 1932-33 famine killed roughly four million Ukrainians (Holodomor) and 1.5 million Kazakhs; the regime won political control of the countryside but Soviet grain output did not regain 1928 levels for decades.

practice_questions.text: ‘Stalin pursued collectivisation mainly to fund the Five Year Plans.’ Evaluate this view. You should consider economic needs, political motivations and other relevant factors, and reach a substantiated judgement.

Arguments for political and ideological motives:
• Crushing kulaks eliminated the rural class Stalin saw as a threat to socialism.
• Collectivisation reasserted state control over the countryside that Lenin’s NEP had relaxed.

Reach a substantiated overall judgement — e.g. the economic logic was real, but collectivisation also extended Stalin’s political power, defeating Bukharin and giving the regime control of the countryside that the Tsars had never achieved.

lessons.title: The Five Year Plans and Soviet Society
lessons.description: Magnitogorsk, Stakhanovites, Soviet women workers and the human price of headline output targets.
lessons.content_html:
In ten years, the Soviet Union became the world’s third-largest industrial economy. Cities, dams, blast furnaces and metro lines were built almost from scratch. The cost was paid in long shifts, accidents, gulag labour and the rationing of food during the 1932-33 famine. To answer ‘were the Five Year Plans a success?’ in the exam, you have to weigh the headline tonnage gains against the quality, the people and the price.

Aims of the Five Year Plans

Stalin set out three core aims for industrialisation. First, build heavy industry — coal, iron, steel, oil — the foundation of any modern economy. Second, achieve autarky: the USSR must produce inside its own borders everything it might need. Third, prepare for war. Stalin told a 1931 audience: ‘We are fifty or a hundred years behind the advanced countries. We must close this gap in ten years. Either we do it, or they crush us.’

First Five Year Plan, 1928-1932

The First Five Year Plan prioritised coal, steel, oil and electricity. Targets were unrealistic; results in heavy industry were nevertheless dramatic. Coal output rose from 35 to 64 million tonnes, steel from 4 to 6 million tonnes, electricity nearly tripled. Consumer goods barely registered. Showcase projects launched in this period include Magnitogorsk — a giant steel city built in the Urals from 1929, designed by American engineers, peopled in part by deported peasants — and the Dnieper Dam, opened in 1932 as Europe’s largest hydroelectric station.

Second Five Year Plan, 1933-1937

The Second Plan continued heavy industry but added transport (the Moscow Metro opened in 1935) and consumer goods. Mining and engineering grew rapidly. Steel hit roughly 18 million tonnes by 1937. Showcase achievements: the White Sea Canal, dug almost entirely by gulag prisoners with around 25,000 deaths during construction, and the Moscow Metro, with stations made deliberately monumental as a public showcase of socialism.

Third Five Year Plan, 1938-1941

The Third Plan turned to armaments and was interrupted by Operation Barbarossa in June 1941. Tank, aircraft and weapons production became a priority — a shift that paid off when the German invasion came. By 1940, military spending had risen to almost a third of state expenditure.

Key Fact

Each Plan had a showcase project. First Plan: Magnitogorsk and the Dnieper Dam. Second Plan: the White Sea Canal (gulag-built) and the Moscow Metro. Third Plan: tank and aircraft production for the coming war.

Workers’ Lives

Soviet workers paid for the Plans in long hours, brutal discipline and frequent accidents. Lateness of more than 20 minutes became a criminal offence in 1940. Internal passports from December 1932 controlled urban residence; collective farmers could not leave the kolkhoz without permission. Wages were tied to output through piece-rates. Crash construction meant accidents were endemic and quality was poor — whole factories were built on bog, while others produced steel that rusted within months.

Yet propaganda celebrated the worker as the hero of socialism. In August 1935, the miner Alexei Stakhanov reportedly cut 102 tonnes of coal in a single shift — fourteen times the norm. The figure was real but engineered: he had teams clearing the coal away. The myth that grew around him — the Stakhanovite movement — pressured workers to exceed norms, with rewards (housing, holidays, bonuses) for top performers and risks for those who fell behind.

The Plans drew women into industry on a scale unseen elsewhere. Female factory employment rose from about 3 million in 1928 to 13 million by 1940; women became a majority of the medical profession. State nurseries, free education and literacy programmes lifted women’s status in real ways. The 1936 Constitution proclaimed equality. Yet women still did the cooking, queuing and childcare on top of their factory shift — the ‘double burden’. Family law tightened in 1936: abortion was banned and divorce made harder, partly to drive up the birth rate after the famine.

City Dwellers and Professionals

The 1920s urban culture of free speech and open debate was crushed. New apartment blocks went up, but the housing shortage meant most workers lived in barracks or shared single rooms in ‘communal’ flats. Professionals — engineers, doctors, planners — were given privileges (better housing, dachas, food access) but were also targeted in ‘wrecking’ trials when projects went wrong, including the Shakhty trial of 1928 that scapegoated mining engineers for the failures of the First Plan.

Were the Plans a Success?

Examiner reports flag this as the recurring weak point in answers. The honest answer is: depends on the metric.

In headline tonnage, yes. By 1940 the USSR was a major industrial power, the world’s third-largest after the US and Germany. The Plans gave the country the steel and weapons that survived Barbarossa. Against the metric of preparing for war — Stalin’s explicit aim — they worked. But quality was often poor: tractors broke; steel cracked; new plants ran far below capacity. Quotas were sometimes met by including gulag output and falsifying figures. Consumer goods (clothes, shoes, kitchenware) remained scarce throughout the 1930s. The Plans were a triumph of headline numbers and a failure of living standards. Top-band 12-mark answers reach a substantiated overall judgement that names which metric they are weighing — not just ‘successful in some ways and not in others’.

Key Fact

By 1940, Soviet industrial output had roughly tripled and the USSR was the world’s third-largest economy. But headline tonnage gains hid quality failures, gulag labour disguised in totals, and consumer poverty. The Plans succeeded against Stalin’s war-preparation aim and failed against worker living standards.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 12-mark Period Essays on whether the Plans succeeded, examiner reports praise students who name the metric they are weighing — tonnage, war preparation, living standards, quality — rather than concluding ‘successful in some ways and not others’. For 8-mark Evaluate an Interpretation, totalitarian readings (Stalin personally drove the modernisation) clash with revisionist accounts that stress workers, foreign engineers and forced labourers. Always cite a specific tonnage, project name (Magnitogorsk, Dnieper Dam, White Sea Canal) or year — precision earns marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Five Year Plans (1928-1941) prioritised heavy industry, autarky and war preparation; showcase projects included Magnitogorsk, the Dnieper Dam, the White Sea Canal and the Moscow Metro.
  • Soviet workers faced harsh discipline, internal passports, and the Stakhanovite pressure to exceed norms; women entered industry in huge numbers but still carried a ‘double burden’ at home.
  • By 1940 the USSR was the world’s third-largest industrial economy — but headline tonnage hid quality failures, gulag labour and consumer poverty.

lessons.title: Terror, Purges and the Cult of Stalin
lessons.description: Show trials, the NKVD, the gulag, censorship and the propaganda image of Stalin as the great leader.
lessons.content_html:
Between 1936 and 1938 Stalin systematically destroyed his own party, his army officer corps, and millions of ordinary citizens. The peak years of the Great Terror — sometimes called the ‘Yezhovshchina’ — saw roughly 750,000 people shot and over a million sent to forced-labour camps. Why this happened, and how much was Stalin’s personal will, is one of the most contested questions in Soviet history.

The Trigger: the Murder of Kirov

On 1 December 1934, Sergei Kirov, the popular Leningrad party chief, was shot dead at the Smolny Institute by a young dissident, Leonid Nikolaev. Stalin used the murder as proof that hidden enemies were active inside the party. The same day, a decree authorised summary trials and execution of suspected terrorists. Whether Stalin himself ordered the killing remains debated — the totalitarian school argues yes, revisionists say a deranged loner is sufficient. Either way, Kirov’s death triggered the wave of arrests that culminated in the Great Terror.

The Show Trials of the Old Bolsheviks, 1936-1938

Between August 1936 and March 1938, three great Moscow show trials destroyed the surviving leadership of the October Revolution.

  • August 1936 — the ‘Trial of the Sixteen’: Zinoviev, Kamenev and 14 others confessed to plotting with Trotsky to murder Stalin and Kirov. All were shot.
  • January 1937 — the ‘Trial of the Seventeen’: Karl Radek and Yuri Pyatakov among them. Most shot.
  • March 1938 — the ‘Trial of the Twenty-One’: Bukharin, the leading Bolshevik intellectual and former defender of the NEP, confessed and was executed. So was Yagoda, the former NKVD chief.

Confessions were extracted by sleep deprivation, threats to families and prolonged interrogation. The trials were a public theatre: foreign journalists were allowed in to watch defendants admit to fantastic crimes. Western observers split — some accepted the confessions, others (including the philosopher John Dewey’s commission) denounced them as fabrications. Modern historians treat the confessions as forced.

Key Fact

Three Moscow show trials destroyed the Old Bolshevik leadership: the Trial of the Sixteen (Aug 1936, Zinoviev and Kamenev shot), the Trial of the Seventeen (Jan 1937), and the Trial of the Twenty-One (Mar 1938, Bukharin shot). Confessions were extracted by torture and threats to families.

Purge of the Red Army

In June 1937, Marshal Mikhail Tukhachevsky and seven other senior generals were tried in secret and shot, accused of plotting with Nazi Germany. The purge then ran through the officer corps. Of the Red Army’s eight marshals, five were shot. Of 80 senior army commanders, 75 were executed or imprisoned. Around 35,000 officers in total — perhaps a third of the corps — were removed. The damage was visible four years later: the early disasters of Operation Barbarossa in 1941 partly reflected an army shorn of its experienced leadership.

The NKVD, Yezhov and the Gulag

The institutional driver was the NKVD (the People’s Commissariat for Internal Affairs), heir to the Cheka. From September 1936 it was led by Nikolai Yezhov — the ‘Yezhovshchina’ takes its name from him. Yezhov set quotas for arrests by region: each NKVD office had a target number of ‘enemies’ to find. Quotas drove denunciations as ordinary Soviets accused colleagues, neighbours and rivals to deflect attention from themselves.

Most arrested were sent to the gulag: a network of forced-labour camps stretching from Solovki to Kolyma in the Soviet Far East. Conditions were brutal — mining gold or felling timber on starvation rations in Arctic temperatures. Estimates of camp deaths in the late 1930s vary; perhaps a million died of cold, hunger and overwork. By 1939 the gulag held around 1.6 million prisoners and was a significant economic asset, building canals, railways and mines.

Yezhov himself was arrested in November 1938 and shot in 1940. Lavrenti Beria replaced him and wound the Terror down somewhat, though arrests and shootings continued. The pattern — Stalin discarding his own enforcers when they became too associated with the violence — would repeat.

The Terror was not limited to old revolutionaries. Mass operations targeted entire categories: ex-kulaks deported in 1929-30, Polish residents of the USSR (around 110,000 shot in the ‘Polish Operation’ of 1937-38), Germans, Latvians and other minorities, plus engineers, priests and teachers. Roughly 750,000 people were executed in 1936-38, with another million-plus sent to camps. Examiner reports flag students who write ‘only old Bolsheviks were purged’ — this is wrong and loses marks.

Censorship, Socialist Realism and the Cult of Personality

A controlled culture sat alongside the violence. Socialist Realism became the only permitted style in 1934: novels, paintings, films and music had to portray heroic workers, wise leaders and a glorious socialist future. Modernist and experimental art was condemned as ‘formalist’. Photographs were retouched to remove disgraced figures — Trotsky was airbrushed out of pictures of Lenin’s funeral; Yezhov was airbrushed out alongside Stalin once he too was purged. School textbooks rewrote the history of the revolution to put Stalin alongside Lenin.

The cult of personality reached its peak. Stalin’s portraits hung in every classroom, factory and kolkhoz. Streets, cities and a tank model bore his name. The 1936 Constitution proclaimed the most democratic political system in the world — a paper document, since real power lay with Stalin and the Politburo. The cult was not just imposed: ordinary Soviets, including many who lost relatives in the Terror, often genuinely believed Stalin was being deceived by NKVD officials acting on their own authority.

Why? The Historiography

Why did the Terror happen? The two main schools clash sharply.

The totalitarian school, led by Robert Conquest in *The Great Terror* (1968), argues the Purges were driven top-down by Stalin’s personal will to remove rivals and consolidate power. The Terror was deliberate, planned, and centrally directed. Revisionists, led by J. Arch Getty (*Origins of the Great Purges*, 1985) and Sheila Fitzpatrick, argue the Terror grew partly out of bureaucratic chaos, denunciations from below, and conflict between Moscow and the regions. Stalin set the tone, but quotas and local activists shaped the scale. Both schools agree Stalin was responsible — they disagree on whether the violence was a centrally controlled machine or a chain reaction Stalin lost control of and only later contained. Top-band 8-mark Evaluate an Interpretation answers can name these schools and use them to test which view a given source is drawing on.

Key Fact

The totalitarian school (Conquest) argues the Terror was driven top-down by Stalin’s personal will. Revisionists (Fitzpatrick, Getty) argue it grew partly from quota culture, denunciations from below and bureaucratic chaos — though Stalin set the political climate that allowed it.

lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The murder of Kirov in December 1934 triggered the Great Terror; three Moscow show trials (1936, 1937, 1938) destroyed the Old Bolshevik leadership including Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin.
  • The Red Army was decapitated in 1937 (Tukhachevsky and the senior officer corps), with consequences for Soviet performance in 1941; the NKVD under Yezhov ran the gulag and shot roughly 750,000 people in 1936-38.
  • Socialist Realism, censorship and the cult of personality controlled culture; historiography splits between Conquest’s totalitarian reading and the revisionist account from Fitzpatrick and Getty.

lessons.title: The Great Patriotic War, 1941-1945
lessons.description: Operation Barbarossa, Stalingrad, factory evacuation east and the staggering cost of victory.
lessons.content_html:
For four years from June 1941 the Soviet Union fought the largest land war in history. Roughly 27 million Soviet citizens died — about one in seven. By 1945 Stalin was master of half of Europe and a co-architect of the post-war world. The story of the Great Patriotic War is one of catastrophic early losses, brutal endurance, and a transformation of Stalin’s rule that combined wartime relaxation with renewed terror after victory.

The Nazi-Soviet Pact, 1939

In August 1939, Stalin and Hitler stunned the world by signing the Nazi-Soviet Pact, a non-aggression treaty negotiated by Foreign Minister Vyacheslav Molotov and his German counterpart Joachim von Ribbentrop. Secret protocols divided Eastern Europe into spheres of influence: Stalin took eastern Poland, the Baltic states and parts of Romania; Hitler took western Poland and a free hand against the West. Stalin saw the Pact as buying time and pushing the Soviet border westwards. Hitler always intended to break it.

Operation Barbarossa, June 1941

Stalin received dozens of warnings of an imminent German attack — from British intelligence, his own spies (Richard Sorge in Tokyo, Leopold Trepper’s Red Orchestra), and his front-line generals. He dismissed them as British provocations. On 22 June 1941, three million German and Axis soldiers crossed the Soviet frontier in Operation Barbarossa. The Luftwaffe destroyed most of the Soviet air force on the ground in 24 hours.

Stalin reportedly withdrew to his dacha for several days, possibly expecting to be arrested by his own Politburo. When he eventually addressed the nation by radio on 3 July, he called Soviet citizens ‘brothers and sisters’ — family language not used in Stalin propaganda before. By December 1941 the Germans had reached the suburbs of Moscow. Three million Soviet soldiers had been killed or captured.

Key Fact

Operation Barbarossa launched on 22 June 1941 with three million Axis troops. Stalin had ignored intelligence warnings and the 1937 purges had stripped the army of experienced commanders. By December 1941, three million Soviet soldiers had been killed or captured, and the Germans were at the gates of Moscow.

Mobilising the Home Front

The most dramatic Soviet achievement was industrial. Between July and December 1941, around 1,500 factories were dismantled and shipped east of the Ural Mountains, beyond the reach of German bombers. Workers, mostly women, restarted production on muddy ground in the Urals winter. By 1942, Soviet weapons output exceeded German output. The T-34 tank — faster, better-armoured and easier to produce than its German rivals — became the iconic Soviet weapon of the war.

Female employment surged again. Women drove tractors, ran lathes, served as pilots in the ‘Night Witches’ bomber regiment, and worked as front-line snipers and medics. Around half a million women served in the Red Army. American Lend-Lease — trucks, food, aviation fuel, raw materials — helped: the USSR received over 400,000 trucks and roughly 14,000 aircraft. The relative weight of Lend-Lease versus Soviet production is debated; both mattered.

Leningrad, Stalingrad and Kursk

The siege of Leningrad ran from September 1941 to January 1944 — 872 days. Roughly one million civilians died, mostly of starvation; people ate wallpaper paste, leather and, in extreme cases, the dead. The Battle of Stalingrad, between August 1942 and February 1943, became the war’s turning point. German Sixth Army, encircled by a Soviet pincer movement (Operation Uranus, November 1942), surrendered on 2 February 1943 under Field Marshal Friedrich Paulus — 91,000 prisoners of whom only 5,000 survived to return home in the 1950s.

The Battle of Kursk in July 1943, the largest tank engagement in history, confirmed Soviet superiority. From there, Soviet forces drove west, reaching Berlin in April 1945. Stalin signed the German surrender on 9 May 1945 — Victory Day, still Russia’s most important national holiday.

Stalin’s record as a wartime leader is contested. Early failures — ignoring intelligence, paralysis at Barbarossa, ordering ‘not one step back’ (Order 227 of July 1942) which forbade retreat at Stalingrad on pain of death — cost millions of Soviet lives. Later, he learned to delegate to professionals like Marshal Georgy Zhukov, the most successful Red Army commander, who oversaw victories at Moscow, Stalingrad, Kursk and Berlin. Stalin chaired the State Defence Committee that ran the war effort and made the strategic decisions on factory evacuation. Examiner reports flag the ‘Stalin was always brilliant’ misconception — show you can weigh the early failures against the eventual victory.

Wartime Society

War transformed daily life. Stalin tactically relaxed pressure on the Russian Orthodox Church — reopening churches, releasing imprisoned bishops — to mobilise patriotic feeling. Wartime propaganda emphasised Russian rather than Communist heroes (Alexander Nevsky, Suvorov) and used the term ‘Motherland’ (Rodina) more than ‘socialism’. The Comintern was dissolved in 1943 to reassure the Western Allies. Conditions for ordinary Soviets remained brutal: rationing, conscription, deportation of suspect minorities (Chechens, Crimean Tatars, Volga Germans) en masse. Famines hit again in 1942-43.

Repression continued alongside this relaxation. Order 270 in 1941 declared every Soviet soldier who surrendered to the enemy a traitor; their families could be punished. SMERSH (counter-intelligence under the NKVD) shot deserters and screened returning prisoners of war. The gulag continued to expand. Wartime relaxation was tactical, not principled — once victory was secured, much of it would be reversed.

From 1941 onwards Stalin deported entire ethnic groups suspected of disloyalty. Volga Germans were uprooted in 1941 within weeks of Barbarossa. Chechens and Ingush were deported from the North Caucasus in February 1944 — around half a million people moved by cattle truck to Kazakhstan and Central Asia in days, with thousands dying of cold and hunger en route. The Crimean Tatars followed in May 1944, accused of collaborating with the German occupiers; nearly a third died in the first year of exile. The deportations show the wartime regime continuing the pre-war logic of collective punishment, even as it relaxed pressure on the Orthodox Church for tactical reasons.

The Cost of Victory

By 1945 the USSR had paid a price beyond comparison. Roughly 27 million Soviet dead, perhaps two-thirds of them civilians. About 1,700 cities and 70,000 villages were destroyed. Industry had to be rebuilt from rubble across European Russia, Ukraine and Belarus. Yet the Soviet Union emerged a superpower — with the Red Army occupying Eastern Europe, atomic-weapon research underway, and a permanent seat on the UN Security Council. Stalin was at the height of his international authority. Within a year of victory the wartime alliance with Britain and the United States had collapsed into the Cold War.

Key Fact

The Soviet Union lost roughly 27 million people in the war — about one in seven citizens. The siege of Leningrad lasted 872 days; the German Sixth Army surrendered at Stalingrad on 2 February 1943. The cost was matched by transformation: the USSR emerged a superpower controlling Eastern Europe.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Examiner reports flag two recurring misconceptions on this period. Don’t write ‘Stalin was always a brilliant wartime leader’ — show you know about Order 227 and the Barbarossa paralysis. Don’t write ‘the USSR won because of Allied aid alone’ — Lend-Lease mattered, but factory evacuation east and Soviet manpower were decisive. For 8-mark Evaluate an Interpretation, name historiographical positions: orthodox Soviet readings stress the heroism of the Soviet people; Western readings (some critical, some respectful) weigh Stalin’s role against the Red Army and the home front.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Nazi-Soviet Pact (August 1939) bought Stalin time but Operation Barbarossa (June 1941) caught him off guard; three million Soviet soldiers were killed or captured by December 1941.
  • Soviet survival rested on the eastward evacuation of around 1,500 factories, the role of women in industry and the army, and a tactical relaxation of repression that included reopening Orthodox churches and dropping ‘socialism’ for ‘Motherland’ in propaganda.
  • By 1945 the USSR was a superpower at staggering cost: roughly 27 million dead, 1,700 cities destroyed, and Eastern Europe under Soviet control as the Cold War began.

• Stalin’s mistakes — ignoring Barbarossa warnings, paralysis in June 1941, Order 227 — nearly lost the war.

glossary_terms.definition: The Soviet term for the Second World War on the Eastern Front, 1941-1945, fought against Nazi Germany.
The August 1939 non-aggression treaty between Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union, with secret protocols dividing Eastern Europe into spheres of influence.
The German invasion of the Soviet Union launched on 22 June 1941, the largest military operation in history.
The 872-day German siege of Leningrad, September 1941 to January 1944, in which roughly one million civilians died, mostly of starvation.
The Soviet name for 9 May 1945, when Nazi Germany formally surrendered to the Red Army; remains a major Russian holiday.
